chunks.title: API
chunks.text: A fixed menu of requests one program offers to another. The app uses the backend's API to ask for the menu, place orders, and so on — it can only ask for things on the menu.

chunks.title: Backend
chunks.text: The program running on a server that does the real work and enforces the rules — the 'brain'. The app can't be trusted; the backend can.

chunks.title: Frontend
chunks.text: The part a person actually sees and touches — here, the mobile app. Its job is to show things and ask for things.

chunks.title: Server
chunks.text: A computer in a data centre that runs all the time and answers requests over the internet. Your backend runs on one.

chunks.title: Client
chunks.text: Whoever is making the request — usually the app on a customer's phone. 'Never trust the client' means the phone can be tampered with, so the backend re-checks everything.

chunks.title: Database
chunks.text: The part that remembers things permanently — through restarts and crashes. Every order and customer lives here.

chunks.title: Table
chunks.text: One kind of thing in the database, like a strict spreadsheet. The Order table holds all orders, one per row.

chunks.title: Row
chunks.text: One single item in a table — one order, one user.

chunks.title: Column
chunks.text: One fact about each row — an order's total, its status.

chunks.title: Foreign key
chunks.text: A column that points at a row in another table. An order's user_id points at the User who placed it — that's how tables link together.

chunks.title: Primary key
chunks.text: The unique id that identifies one row, so you can always find exactly it.

chunks.title: Index
chunks.text: A pre-sorted lookup, like the index at the back of a book. It lets the database jump straight to matching rows instead of reading every one.

chunks.title: Query
chunks.text: A question you ask the database — 'give me this store's pending orders'.

chunks.title: SQL
chunks.text: The language for asking a relational database questions. You describe what you want; the database figures out how to get it.

chunks.title: Transaction
chunks.text: A group of writes that all succeed together or all undo together. There's no half-finished state — the bedrock of handling money safely.

chunks.title: ACID
chunks.text: Four guarantees a serious database makes: writes are all-or-nothing, rules are never left broken, simultaneous work doesn't collide, and once saved it survives a crash.

chunks.title: Migration
chunks.text: A versioned, repeatable change to the database's shape (a new column or table), so the structure evolves safely instead of by hand.

chunks.title: ORM
chunks.text: A translator between your code's objects and the database's rows, so you read/write data without hand-writing SQL. Prisma is the one here.

chunks.title: Decimal
chunks.text: An exact number type used for money, so amounts like ₹0.10 are stored precisely — unlike ordinary computer 'floats', which can't.

chunks.title: Schema
chunks.text: The blueprint that describes every table, column, and link in the database. Here it's one file: schema.prisma.

chunks.title: Referential integrity
chunks.text: The database's promise that a link always points at something real — you can't have an order item for a product that doesn't exist.

chunks.title: HTTP
chunks.text: The request-and-reply language of the web. The app sends a request; the backend sends back a response. The app always asks first.

chunks.title: REST
chunks.text: A tidy convention for organising a web API around 'resources' (orders, products) addressed by clean URLs and standard verbs (GET to read, POST to create).

chunks.title: Endpoint
chunks.text: One specific address + action in an API, like 'GET /api/v1/menu' — a single thing you can ask for.

chunks.title: Request
chunks.text: A message the app sends to the backend asking for something or sending something.

chunks.title: Response
chunks.text: The backend's reply to a request — the data, plus a status code saying how it went.

chunks.title: JSON
chunks.text: A simple text way to write down structured data (objects and lists), understood by every language. It's the shape data travels in.

chunks.title: JWT
chunks.text: A 'JSON Web Token' — a tamper-proof badge the backend issues at login that says 'this is who I am', signed with a secret only the server knows.

chunks.title: Cookie
chunks.text: A small piece of data the browser stores and sends back automatically on each request — here it carries your signed login token.

chunks.title: httpOnly
chunks.text: A cookie setting meaning JavaScript on the page cannot read it. So even a malicious injected script can't steal your login.

chunks.title: CSRF
chunks.text: Cross-Site Request Forgery — an attack where another website quietly fires a request to your backend riding your cookie. A CSRF token blocks it.

chunks.title: Token
chunks.text: A small string that stands in for something — proof of who you are, or a one-time key. Tokens here include the login JWT and the CSRF token.

chunks.title: Header
chunks.text: Extra info attached to a request or response — the auth cookie, the content type, a request id — sitting alongside the main data.

chunks.title: Status code
chunks.text: A number in the reply saying how it went: 200 OK, 401 not logged in, 404 not found, 500 the server broke.

chunks.title: Stateless
chunks.text: The backend keeps no memory of you between requests — your identity rides in your token each time. That's what lets many copies of it run at once.

chunks.title: Session
chunks.text: The idea of 'you, currently logged in'. Here it's carried in a signed cookie rather than stored on the server.

chunks.title: SSE
chunks.text: Server-Sent Events — one long-lived connection the server uses to push small 'something changed' nudges to the app, so the screen can update live.

chunks.title: Webhook
chunks.text: When an outside service (like a payment gateway) calls your backend to tell it something happened, instead of you having to keep asking.

chunks.title: Flutter
chunks.text: The toolkit the app is built with. It draws every pixel itself, so the app looks identical on iPhone and Android from one codebase.

chunks.title: Widget
chunks.text: Flutter's building block. Everything on screen is a widget, and screens are just bigger widgets made of smaller ones — like Lego.

chunks.title: Dart
chunks.text: The programming language the app is written in — typed and 'null-safe', designed to pair with Flutter.

chunks.title: State
chunks.text: Anything that can change while the app is open — what's in your cart, which filter is on. Managing it well is what keeps the screen consistent.

chunks.title: Provider
chunks.text: In Riverpod, a named place that holds a piece of shared state (like the cart) so any part of the screen can read the same truth.

chunks.title: Riverpod
chunks.text: The library the app uses to hold and share state, so different parts of the screen never disagree about the cart or the filters.

chunks.title: Reactive
chunks.text: When something recomputes itself automatically the moment its inputs change — change one value and the screen redraws, with no manual syncing.

chunks.title: Repository
chunks.text: The one place that knows how to fetch a kind of data (the menu). Screens ask it for 'the menu' without knowing any URLs.

chunks.title: Dependency injection
chunks.text: Instead of a piece of code creating its own tools, it's handed them. That makes it easy to swap a real tool for a fake one in tests.

chunks.title: Interceptor
chunks.text: Code that runs automatically on every network request/response — attaching the login cookie, adding a trace id, retrying a blip — so no screen has to.

chunks.title: Dio
chunks.text: The app's single network client. Every request to the backend goes through it, which is where interceptors do their work.

chunks.title: Null safety
chunks.text: A language feature that forces you to say whether a value can be 'nothing'. It kills the classic 'it was empty and the app crashed' bug.

chunks.title: Node.js
chunks.text: The thing that lets JavaScript run on a server. Your backend is a Node program. It's great at handling many requests that are mostly waiting.

chunks.title: Express
chunks.text: A small framework for Node that maps each URL to the right code and runs 'middleware' guards along the way.

chunks.title: Middleware
chunks.text: Code that runs before the main handler, on every matching request — checking auth, verifying a CSRF token — and can stop a bad request cold.

chunks.title: Route
chunks.text: The rule that says 'a request to this URL with this method runs this function'. The front desk of the backend.

chunks.title: Service
chunks.text: Where the real logic lives (fetch the catalogue, apply prices). Routes stay thin and call services, so the logic is testable on its own.

chunks.title: Event loop
chunks.text: Node's single line of work that never sits idle waiting. It hands off slow jobs and serves other requests meanwhile — like one waiter juggling many tables.

chunks.title: Idempotency
chunks.text: Doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once. A retried 'place order' is recognised as a repeat and charges you only once.

chunks.title: Ledger
chunks.text: Tracking points or money as an append-only list of every movement (like a bank statement), so the balance is the running total and nothing can be lost.

chunks.title: Append-only
chunks.text: You only ever add new rows, never edit or delete old ones. That's what makes a history trustworthy — it can't be quietly rewritten.

chunks.title: State machine
chunks.text: A thing that's always in exactly one of a fixed set of states, where only certain moves are allowed — so impossible situations can't happen.

chunks.title: Optimistic concurrency
chunks.text: A version number on a row so two requests changing it at once can't both win — the second notices it changed and backs off.

chunks.title: Race condition
chunks.text: A bug where two things happen at the same instant and collide on the same data, producing a wrong result (like spending the same points twice).

chunks.title: Cache
chunks.text: A ready-made copy of an expensive answer (like the menu), kept close by so most requests are served instantly instead of recomputed.

chunks.title: Cache invalidation
chunks.text: Throwing away a cached copy when the real data changes, so you don't keep serving a stale price. Famously the hard part of caching.

chunks.title: Queue
chunks.text: A line of messages for slow or external work. The backend drops a job on it and replies instantly; a separate worker handles the job later.

chunks.title: Worker
chunks.text: A separate process that picks jobs off a queue and does the slow work (sending emails, notifying the kitchen) in the background.

chunks.title: Load balancer
chunks.text: One public 'door' that spreads incoming requests across many identical copies of the backend, so traffic can grow by adding copies.

chunks.title: Horizontal scaling
chunks.text: Handling more load by running more copies of the same thing, rather than one ever-bigger machine. Statelessness is what makes it possible.

chunks.title: CDN
chunks.text: A network of servers around the world that keep copies of images/files close to users, so they load fast everywhere.

chunks.title: Redis
chunks.text: A very fast in-memory store often used as a shared cache that all backend copies read from.

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.text: Being able to see what your running system is doing — logs, metrics, and traces — so you can find a problem before customers tell you.

chunks.title: Request id
chunks.text: A unique tag attached to each request so you can follow one order's whole journey across every part of the system.

chunks.title: Refine
chunks.text: A framework that generates the admin panel's repetitive screens (list, create, edit, view) so they don't have to be hand-built.

chunks.title: CRUD
chunks.text: Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four basic things you do to data, and the four screens an admin panel mostly needs.

chunks.title: Next.js
chunks.text: The framework behind the admin panel (and this site). It adds routing, server rendering, and a build system on top of React.

chunks.title: React
chunks.text: A library for building web interfaces out of reusable 'components' — the web equivalent of Flutter's widgets.

chunks.title: Component
chunks.text: A reusable piece of UI that renders itself from data — a button, a table, a card. You build pages by composing them.

chunks.title: Server rendering
chunks.text: Building a page's HTML on the server so it arrives ready-to-show and fast, instead of a blank page that fills in later.

chunks.title: Docker
chunks.text: A way to pack an app together with everything it needs into one sealed 'container' that runs identically on any machine.

chunks.title: Kubernetes
chunks.text: A manager for many containers — it runs them, restarts crashed ones, and adds or removes copies as load changes.

chunks.title: CI/CD
chunks.text: Automatically testing every change and then deploying it — so broken code is caught before it ships, and shipping is routine.

chunks.title: Environment variable
chunks.text: A setting (like the database address or a secret key) supplied to the app from outside the code, so secrets never live in the codebase.

chunks.title: Deploy
chunks.text: To put a new version of the code live on the server where real customers use it.

chunks.title: Infrastructure as code
chunks.text: Describing your servers and database in a file in your repo, so a deploy is reproducible and reviewable instead of clicking around a dashboard.

chunks.title: Latency
chunks.text: How long you wait for a response, usually in milliseconds. Low latency feels instant; high latency feels laggy.

chunks.title: Throughput
chunks.text: How much work a system gets done per second — requests served, orders processed. More throughput, more load handled.

chunks.title: Bottleneck
chunks.text: The one slowest part that caps the whole system's speed, like the narrow neck of a bottle. Fix it and everything speeds up.

chunks.title: Replica
chunks.text: A copy of your database kept in sync with the original, so reads can be spread across many copies and one failure isn't fatal.

chunks.title: Sharding
chunks.text: Splitting one huge database into pieces ('shards') by some key, so no single machine has to hold all of the data.

chunks.title: Eventual consistency
chunks.text: Copies of data may briefly disagree after a change, but given a moment they all settle on the same value. The trade for staying fast and available.

chunks.title: CAP theorem
chunks.text: When the network splits, a distributed store can stay consistent or stay available — not both. You must choose which to sacrifice.

chunks.title: Backpressure
chunks.text: When a system is overwhelmed it pushes back — slowing or rejecting new work — instead of collapsing. A queue filling up is backpressure.

chunks.title: Rate limiting
chunks.text: Capping how many requests one client may make in a window, so nobody (or no runaway bug) can flood the system.

chunks.title: Circuit breaker
chunks.text: A guard that stops calling a failing service for a while, so one sick dependency doesn't drag everything down — like an electrical breaker tripping.

chunks.title: Retry
chunks.text: Trying a failed request again, because many failures are temporary blips. Pair it with backoff and idempotency so retries stay safe.

chunks.title: Exponential backoff
chunks.text: Waiting longer and longer between retries (1s, 2s, 4s…) so a struggling service gets room to recover instead of being hammered.

chunks.title: Saga
chunks.text: A long job split into steps across services, each with an 'undo'. If a later step fails, earlier ones are reversed — consistency without one giant transaction.

chunks.title: Pub/Sub
chunks.text: Publishers post messages to a topic; any number of subscribers receive them. Sender and receiver never have to know about each other.

chunks.title: Message broker
chunks.text: The middleman (like RabbitMQ or Kafka) that reliably carries messages between services, holding them until a worker is ready.

chunks.title: Vertical scaling
chunks.text: Handling more load by making one machine bigger (more CPU/RAM). Simple, but there's a ceiling — eventually you must scale out instead.

chunks.title: TTL
chunks.text: Time To Live — how long a cached copy may be reused before it's considered stale and refetched.

chunks.title: Eviction
chunks.text: Dropping items from a full cache to make room. The policy (often LRU) decides which ones go.

chunks.title: LRU
chunks.text: Least Recently Used — an eviction rule that throws out whatever hasn't been touched for the longest when space runs out.

chunks.title: Thundering herd
chunks.text: A popular cached item expires and thousands of requests miss at once, all stampeding the slow source together.

chunks.title: Blast radius
chunks.text: How much of the system one failure takes down with it. Good design keeps the blast radius small.

chunks.title: Consensus
chunks.text: How a group of machines agree on a single value or order of events, even when some are slow or fail. Raft is one such algorithm.

chunks.title: Quorum
chunks.text: The minimum number of machines that must agree before a decision counts — usually more than half, so two conflicting majorities can't exist.

chunks.title: p99 latency
chunks.text: The latency that 99% of requests beat. It catches the slow tail that averages hide — the 1-in-100 users having a bad time.

chunks.title: SLO / SLA
chunks.text: An SLO is a target you hold yourself to ('99.9% of requests succeed'); an SLA is the promise you make to customers, often with penalties.

chunks.title: MTTR
chunks.text: Mean Time To Recovery — how long, on average, to get back to healthy after an incident. Lower is more resilient.

chunks.title: Encryption
chunks.text: Scrambling data with a key so only someone with the key can read it. Protects data in transit (TLS) and at rest.

chunks.title: Hashing
chunks.text: A one-way scramble of data into a fixed fingerprint. Passwords are stored hashed, so a leak doesn't reveal them.

chunks.title: Salt
chunks.text: Random data added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords don't share a hash and precomputed-attack tables fail.

chunks.title: TLS
chunks.text: The lock on HTTPS. It encrypts traffic between app and server so nobody in between can read or tamper with it.

chunks.title: OAuth
chunks.text: A standard for granting one app limited access to your account on another ('Sign in with Google') without sharing your password.

chunks.title: RBAC
chunks.text: Role-Based Access Control — permissions attached to roles (admin, staff, customer) rather than individuals, so access is easy to reason about.

chunks.title: Least privilege
chunks.text: Give every part of the system only the access it truly needs — so a breach in one place can't reach everything.

chunks.title: XSS
chunks.text: Cross-Site Scripting — sneaking malicious JavaScript into a page so it runs in other users' browsers. Escaping output and a strict CSP stop it.

chunks.title: SQL injection
chunks.text: Tricking the database by smuggling SQL into an input field. Parameterised queries (never gluing strings together) shut it down.

chunks.title: SSRF
chunks.text: Server-Side Request Forgery — tricking your server into making requests to places it shouldn't, like internal-only systems.

chunks.title: Zero trust
chunks.text: Assume no request is safe just because it's 'inside' the network — verify identity and permission on every single call.

chunks.title: DNS
chunks.text: The internet's phone book. It turns a name like burgerfarm.com into the numeric IP address of the server to talk to.

chunks.title: IP address
chunks.text: The numeric address of a machine on a network — a postal address for packets of data.

chunks.title: Port
chunks.text: A numbered door on a machine for a particular service — web traffic uses 80/443, a dev server maybe 3000.

chunks.title: Reverse proxy
chunks.text: A server that sits in front of your backends, taking all incoming requests and forwarding them — handy for TLS, caching and load balancing.

chunks.title: CORS
chunks.text: Browser rules deciding whether a page on one site may call an API on another. The server must explicitly allow it.

chunks.title: WebSocket
chunks.text: A two-way, always-open connection between app and server, so either side can send messages any time — used for live chat and updates.

chunks.title: GraphQL
chunks.text: An API style where the client asks for exactly the fields it wants in one request, instead of hitting many fixed REST endpoints.

chunks.title: gRPC
chunks.text: A fast, typed way for services to call each other using compact binary messages — popular between backend services.

chunks.title: Virtual machine
chunks.text: A whole simulated computer running on shared physical hardware, so one big server can safely host many isolated tenants.

chunks.title: Serverless
chunks.text: You upload a function; the cloud runs it on demand and bills per call. No servers to manage — it scales to zero when idle.

chunks.title: Object storage
chunks.text: Cheap, near-infinite storage for files (images, backups) addressed by a key, like Amazon S3. Not a filesystem, not a database.

chunks.title: Region
chunks.text: A geographic cluster of a cloud's data centres. Running near your users cuts latency; spreading across regions survives disasters.

chunks.title: Autoscaling
chunks.text: The cloud automatically adding copies of your app when traffic rises and removing them when it falls, so you pay for what you use.

chunks.title: NoSQL
chunks.text: Databases that drop strict tables for flexible shapes (documents, key-values, graphs), trading some guarantees for scale and flexibility.

chunks.title: B-tree
chunks.text: The balanced, multi-way tree most database indexes use, so lookups stay fast (few disk reads) even with millions of rows.

chunks.title: Normalization
chunks.text: Organising data so each fact lives in exactly one place, avoiding duplicates that can drift out of sync.

chunks.title: Deadlock
chunks.text: Two transactions each holding what the other needs, both stuck forever. The database detects it and kills one to break the tie.

chunks.title: Connection pool
chunks.text: A reusable set of open database connections, so requests borrow one instead of paying to open a fresh connection each time.

chunks.title: LLM
chunks.text: A Large Language Model — an AI trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next word, which lets it write, summarise and answer.

chunks.title: Embedding
chunks.text: Turning text into a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so similar ideas sit close together — the basis of semantic search.

chunks.title: Vector search
chunks.text: Finding the items whose embeddings are nearest to your query's — closest in meaning, rather than by exact keyword.

chunks.title: RAG
chunks.text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation — fetch relevant documents first, then ask the model to answer using them, so it stays grounded and cites sources.

chunks.title: Transformer
chunks.text: The neural-network design behind modern LLMs. Its 'attention' lets it weigh how much each word relates to every other.

chunks.title: Hallucination
chunks.text: When an AI states something false but confident. Grounding it in real sources (RAG) is the main defence.

chunks.title: Inference
chunks.text: Actually running a trained model to get an answer (as opposed to training it). It's what costs you per request in production.

chunks.title: Big-O
chunks.text: Shorthand for how an algorithm's cost grows as the input grows — O(n) doubles when the data doubles; O(1) doesn't care about size.

chunks.title: Recursion
chunks.text: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller piece, until it hits a simple base case.

chunks.title: Concurrency
chunks.text: Juggling many tasks so they all make progress together (not necessarily at the same instant) — like one cook starting several dishes.

chunks.title: Abstraction
chunks.text: Hiding messy detail behind a simple interface, so you can use a thing without knowing how it works inside.

chunks.title: Coupling
chunks.text: How tightly two pieces of code depend on each other. Loose coupling means you can change one without breaking the other.

chunks.title: Separation of concerns
chunks.text: Giving each part of the system one clear job — who-asks kept separate from who-does — so each can change independently.

chunks.title: Single source of truth
chunks.text: Keeping each fact in exactly one authoritative place, so different parts of the app can never disagree about it.

chunks.title: Dart
chunks.text: The programming language your entire mobile app is written in. Dart is the language Flutter speaks — typed, fast, and built so the same code can run natively on both iPhone and Android. A programming language is just the set of words and rules you use to tell a computer what to do. Your app (apps/mobile-app) is written almost entirely in Dart, a language made by Google specifically to pair with Flutter. Dart is statically typed: you (or the tools) declare that a thing is a number, or a MenuProduct, or a list of strings — and the computer checks those promises *before* the app ever runs. A whole class of typos and mismatches gets caught at your desk instead of on a customer's phone. It has sound null safety, which is a big deal. ‘Null' means ‘nothing here'. In older languages, a value you expected could secretly be nothing, and reading it crashed the app — the infamous ‘null pointer'. Dart forces you to say up front whether something *can* be nothing (String?) or never is (String), so the ‘it was empty and everything exploded' bug largely disappears. Dart exists to solve one specific problem: one team, one codebase, both phones. Building separately for iPhone (Swift) and Android (Kotlin) means writing — and bug-fixing — everything twice. Dart + Flutter lets you write it once. It was also designed *around* UI work: hot reload for fast iteration, AOT compilation for buttery 60fps animations, and a syntax familiar to anyone who's seen JavaScript or Java, so the learning curve is gentle. Types & classes: class MenuProduct { ... } — your own named shapes of data, checked at compile time. Null safety: String? means ‘maybe nothing'; String means ‘always something'. The compiler enforces it. Futures & async/await: How Dart waits for slow things (a network call) without freezing the screen. Isolates: Dart is single-threaded, but heavy work can be shoved onto a separate isolate so the UI stays smooth. Kotlin + Swift: The native route — best possible integration, but two separate apps to build and maintain. JavaScript (React Native): One codebase too, but it drives the phone's native widgets through a bridge; Flutter/Dart instead draws every pixel itself. C# (.NET MAUI): Another cross-platform option; smaller ecosystem for this kind of app than Flutter.

chunks.title: Dart — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Every screen, every provider, every model in the app is Dart. When the menu loads, a Dart class MenuProduct describes each item; an async function awaits the network; null safety guarantees a product's name is never secretly missing. The immutable BurgerCustomization in the burger builder is pure Dart too — a typed, null-safe object that can't be edited in place, only copied. Turn off null safety (as old code did) and here's the bad day: the backend returns a product with no price field, the app reads product.price expecting a number, finds nothing, and crashes to a white screen mid-order. Sound null safety makes the compiler refuse to even build that mistake — you're forced to handle the ‘maybe empty' case on purpose.

chunks.title: TypeScript
chunks.text: JavaScript with a safety net — the language of your backend and admin panel. TypeScript is JavaScript plus types: you label what your data looks like, and a checker catches mismatches before the code ever runs. JavaScript is the language of the web, but it's famously loose — it'll happily let you add a number to a sentence and only complain once something's already gone wrong for a user. TypeScript is JavaScript with an added layer: you describe the *shape* of your data (this is a number, that is an Order with these fields), and a tool checks every line against those descriptions. Crucially, the browser and Node.js don't run TypeScript directly. It gets compiled down to plain JavaScript first (your backend's build step is literally prisma generate && tsc, where tsc is the TypeScript compiler). The types are a tool for *you*; they vanish in the final running code. Your backend (apps/backend) and admin panel (apps/admin-panel) are TypeScript. The .ts extension is the giveaway. On a backend that handles money, ‘it broke for a customer' is expensive. TypeScript moves a huge category of mistakes — a misspelled field, the wrong argument, forgetting a value can be null — from *runtime* (a real user, a real failure) to *compile time* (a red squiggle while you type). It also makes the code self-documenting and refactor-safe: rename a field and the compiler shows you every one of the forty places that need updating, instead of you finding them via production errors. Type annotations: amount: number, order: Order — you spell out what each value is. Interfaces & types: Reusable named shapes, like a blueprint for an ‘Order' object. The compiler (tsc): Reads your .ts, checks the types, and emits plain .js the server can run. Generated types: Prisma auto-generates types from your database schema, so your code knows the exact shape of every table. Plain JavaScript: Less ceremony, no build step — but every type mistake waits to ambush you at runtime. Flow: Facebook's type-checker for JS; TypeScript won the ecosystem battle decisively. A typed language (Go, Java): Types from the ground up, but you leave the vast JavaScript ecosystem behind.

chunks.title: TypeScript — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The backend is written in .ts and built with tsc into a dist/ folder of plain JavaScript that Node runs in production. Prisma generates TypeScript types straight from schema.prisma, so when your code reads an Order, the editor already knows it has a total, a status, and an idempotency_key. That generated link between database and code is why a typo like order.totl is caught instantly, not after a customer's payment misbehaves. Drop the types and rename the database column total to grand_total, but miss one spot in the code. Plain JavaScript ships happily; then a customer checks out and the server reads order.total, gets undefined, and tries to charge undefined rupees. TypeScript would have lit up that exact line in red before you ever committed.

chunks.title: Node.js
chunks.text: The engine that runs your backend's JavaScript on a server. Node.js lets JavaScript run on a server instead of only in a browser — it's the thing your backend code actually executes inside. JavaScript was born inside web browsers. Node.js took the browser's JavaScript engine (Google's V8) and wrapped it so the same language can run on a *server* — a computer in a data centre answering requests. Your backend is a Node.js program. Node's signature trait is its event loop: a single main line of work that never sits idle waiting. When your code asks the database for an order, Node doesn't freeze for those few milliseconds — it sets that request aside, serves other customers, and comes back when the answer arrives. This ‘non-blocking I/O' is why one Node process can juggle thousands of waiting requests at once. That design makes Node a superb fit for an app backend, where almost every request is mostly *waiting* — on the database, on the payment gateway, on the kitchen system. Node was chosen because an ordering backend is I/O-bound, not number-crunching: it spends its time waiting on other systems. The event loop turns all that waiting into capacity to serve more users on the same hardware. There's also a people advantage: the app, admin, and backend can all be JavaScript/TypeScript, so one mental model and one ecosystem (npm) covers the whole stack. V8 engine: Google's JavaScript engine (from Chrome) — turns your JS into fast machine code. Event loop: The single line of execution that hands off slow work and never blocks. npm: The package manager — millions of reusable libraries, including Express and Prisma. Modules: Code split into files that import each other; your app.ts wires them together. Python (Django/Flask): Lovely to write; traditionally blocks on I/O unless you reach for async frameworks. Go: Compiled, brilliant at concurrency; a different language and ecosystem to learn. Java / Spring: Rock-solid enterprise default; heavier and more verbose than Node for this size of app.

chunks.title: Node.js — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The backend is a Node.js app. In development it runs the TypeScript directly via ts-node-dev; in production it runs the compiled node dist/app.js. Express (a Node library) handles the HTTP requests, and Prisma (another) talks to PostgreSQL. Because Node keeps no per-user state in its own memory, you can run many identical copies behind a load balancer — the property that lets the backend scale (Part 09). Node's strength is also its trap: there's one main line of work, so if you do something genuinely CPU-heavy on it (resizing huge images, crunching a giant report) the loop *blocks* — every other customer's request hangs until it finishes. The fix is to push heavy work off to a queue and a separate worker (Part 09), keeping the event loop free to do what it's great at: waiting on many things at once.

chunks.title: Flutter
chunks.text: The toolkit that draws every pixel of your app, the same on iPhone and Android. Flutter is how the app is built: you compose tiny ‘widgets' into screens, and Flutter paints them itself — one codebase, identical on both phones. Flutter is a UI toolkit from Google. Its one giant idea: everything on screen is a ‘widget'. A button is a widget, the row holding three buttons is a widget, the whole menu screen is a widget built from smaller widgets. You build an interface by nesting small widgets into bigger ones, like Lego. Unlike most app frameworks, Flutter doesn't borrow the phone's native buttons — it draws every pixel itself with its own rendering engine. That's why a Flutter app looks and behaves *identically* on iPhone and Android, and why custom designs (like your burger builder's animations) are possible without fighting the platform. You describe *what* the screen should look like for the current data, and Flutter figures out the minimal changes to make it so. Change the data, call build again, Flutter redraws. This is the ‘declarative' style. Flutter was chosen for the same reason as Dart: one codebase, both phones, pixel-perfect control. For an app whose personality lives in its custom motion and layout (the radial burger builder, the animated cart), drawing your own pixels beats wrestling each platform's native widgets. Hot reload makes building fast — tweak a colour, see it in a second — and the declarative model means the UI is always a clean function of your data, which pairs perfectly with Riverpod's reactive state. Widgets: The building blocks. Everything visible (and much that isn't) is a widget. The widget tree: Widgets nested inside widgets, forming the whole screen as a tree. build() method: Each widget describes itself from the current data; Flutter calls it to (re)draw. Rendering engine: Flutter's own painter (Skia/Impeller) that turns the tree into actual pixels at 60fps. React Native: Also one codebase, but drives the OS's native widgets via a JS bridge — less pixel control, more ‘native feel' for free. Native (SwiftUI / Jetpack Compose): Best platform integration; two separate apps to build and keep in sync. A web app in a shell: Cheapest to reuse web code; usually the least app-like feel and performance.

chunks.title: Flutter — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The whole app under apps/mobile-app/lib is Flutter. Screens live in each feature's presentation/ folder as widgets; the menu screen is a widget tree that watches Riverpod providers and rebuilds when the cart or filter changes. The burger builder is Flutter showing off: a burger_stack of layered widgets, positioned by computed geometry and animated with the motion engine — exactly the kind of bespoke UI that ‘draw your own pixels' makes possible. Flutter rebuilds widgets a lot, and that's normally cheap — unless you rebuild a huge subtree on every tiny change. Forget to keep widgets small and const where possible, and a single keystroke in a search box can redraw the entire screen, causing visible jank. The fix is the same discipline as state: rebuild only the small widget that actually changed, which Riverpod's fine-grained watching makes easy.

chunks.title: Riverpod
chunks.text: How the app holds shared, live data — the single source of truth, made reactive. Riverpod keeps important data (the cart, the filters) in one place and lets any widget read it, so the whole screen stays in sync automatically. ‘State' is anything that can change while the app is open — what's in your cart, which category is selected, the search text. Riverpod is the library that holds that state and shares it, so different parts of the screen never disagree about it. The core unit is a provider: a named, shared piece of state or logic. A widget ‘watches' a provider; when the provider's value changes, every watcher rebuilds automatically. You never manually tell three widgets ‘hey, the cart changed' — they're already listening. Riverpod also does derived state: one provider can be computed from others. Your visible product list is derived from the full catalogue, the chosen filter, and the chosen category — change any input and the list recomputes itself. Flutter's built-in setState keeps state trapped inside one widget — fine for a toggle, useless when three separate screens need the same cart. Riverpod was chosen because it makes *shared* and *derived* state effortless, is testable without a running app, catches wiring mistakes at compile time, and rebuilds only the widgets that actually use a changed value. It's the practical enforcement of the most important rule in app state: one source of truth, many readers (Part 02). Provider: A named, shared value or computation — the cart, the active filter, the API client. ref.watch / ref.read: How a widget subscribes to a provider (watch = rebuild on change; read = one-off). Derived providers: Providers built from other providers — e.g. the visible-products list. autoDispose: Providers can clean themselves up when nothing's watching, freeing memory. setState: Built in, dead simple, but state is local to one widget — no sharing. Provider (the older one): Riverpod's predecessor; Riverpod fixes its rough edges (compile-time safety, no BuildContext needed). Bloc: Very structured, event-driven; more boilerplate, great for large teams that want strictness. GetX: Batteries-included and terse; less explicit about where state lives.

chunks.title: Riverpod — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The cart lives in one provider (menu_cart_provider.dart); the floating cart bar and the cart screen both watch it, so they can't fall out of sync. In menu_provider.dart, the active filter and category are their own providers, and menuVisibleProductsProvider derives the on-screen list from all three. Even the network client is a provider (apiClientProvider) — handed to repositories rather than created by them, which is dependency injection in action (Part 02). Abandon the single source of truth and let each widget keep its own copy of the cart. Remove an item and one copy misses the memo: the icon shows 2, the cart page shows 3, the bill charges for 3. That's not cosmetic — it's a money bug, and it's the single most common bug in app development. Riverpod's one-truth-many-readers model makes it structurally impossible.

chunks.title: Express
chunks.text: The backend's traffic system — it decides which code answers which request. Express is the Node library that turns an incoming web request into the right function, running guards (middleware) along the way. When the app sends a request to the backend, *something* has to catch it, figure out what it's asking for, run the right code, and send a reply. That something is Express — a small, popular web framework for Node.js. Express has two core ideas. Routes map a URL + method to a handler: ‘a GET to /api/v1/menu runs this function'. Middleware is code that runs *before* the handler, in a chain — checking auth, verifying a CSRF token, attaching a request-id — and can stop a request dead if something's wrong. A request flows through the middleware chain, reaches its route's handler, and the handler sends a response. That orderly pipeline is the whole shape of the backend. Express was chosen for being minimal and unopinionated: it gives you routing and middleware and gets out of the way, which suits a backend that wants its real logic in well-separated service files rather than dictated by a framework. It's also the most widely-used Node framework on earth, so every problem has been solved before and every library plugs into it. Routes: URL + method → handler. router.get('/menu', ...). Middleware: Functions that run before handlers: auth, CSRF, logging, parsing. They can pass or block. req & res: The request object (what came in) and the response object (what you send back). Routers: Groups of related routes (menu, admin) mounted under a path like /api/v1. Fastify: Similar idea, faster, stricter; smaller (but growing) ecosystem. NestJS: Heavily structured, Angular-style; great for big teams, much more ceremony. Raw Node http: No dependencies at all — but you'd reinvent routing and middleware yourself.

chunks.title: Express — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: app.ts creates the Express app and wires in global middleware (security headers, CSRF, request tracing). Route files under src/routes map URLs to handlers; the handlers stay thin and call services (src/services) that hold the real logic. Guards like requireAdmin and requireCsrf live in src/middleware. Everything is mounted under /api/v1, the version prefix that lets the API evolve without breaking old app versions (Part 09). Forget an error-handling middleware and let one handler throw an unexpected error. Without a safety net, that error can crash the whole Node process — taking down *every* customer's request, not just the one that failed. A proper error middleware catches it, logs it, and returns a clean 500 to just that one request while everyone else keeps ordering.

chunks.title: PostgreSQL
chunks.text: The permanent, reliable memory where every order and payment truly lives. PostgreSQL is the relational database that stores Burger Farm's data in linked tables, with hard guarantees that money and orders are never corrupted. A database is the part of the system that *remembers* — permanently, through restarts and crashes. PostgreSQL (‘Postgres') is a relational database: it stores data in tables of rows and columns, like very strict spreadsheets, where one order is one row in the Order table. ‘Relational' means the tables are linked. An order points to the user who placed it and the store it's from; it owns a list of order-items, each pointing to a product. Those links are enforced — you can't have an order-item pointing at a product that doesn't exist. The database simply refuses. Postgres also guarantees ACID transactions: a group of writes either all happen or none do. That's the bedrock that makes it safe to handle money — there's no universe where a payment is recorded but its order vanishes. Burger Farm's data is deeply *related* (orders ↔ users ↔ stores ↔ products) and involves *money*, which demands exact decimals and real transactions. Postgres provides relationships, referential integrity, ACID transactions, and battle-tested decimal math — precisely the guarantees money needs. It's also open-source, endlessly capable (JSON columns, full-text search, geospatial), and trusted by enormous companies — so it scales with you instead of being outgrown. Tables, rows, columns: The grid. One Order row holds one order's total, status, timestamps. Foreign keys: A column that points at another table's row — Order.user_id → User. Links, enforced. Indexes: Pre-sorted lookups (@@index([store_id, status])) that make queries instant at scale. Transactions (ACID): All-or-nothing groups of writes — the core of safely handling money. MySQL: The other big relational database; comparable, slightly different feature set and history. MongoDB (NoSQL): Stores flexible documents, no fixed schema; weaker at the cross-table relationships and transactions an order system leans on. SQLite: A whole database in a single file — perfect for tiny/local apps, not a multi-user server. Firebase/Firestore: Great realtime + easy start, but the truth-and-transactions an ordering backend needs fit a relational DB better.

chunks.title: PostgreSQL — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Every model in schema.prisma becomes a Postgres table: Order, OrderItem, OrderPayment, Product, LoyaltyTransaction, and more. Money columns use Decimal(10,2) for exactness; idempotency_key is marked unique to block double-charges; indexes like @@index([store_id, status]) keep ‘this store's pending orders' instant. Placing an order wraps several writes in a transaction so it's all-or-nothing — the guarantee explored in Part 05 and the order-journey simulator. Strip out the constraints and transactions for ‘speed'. Now a crash mid-checkout leaves an order with no payment (free food) or a payment with no order (a charge for nothing), and a bug can insert an order-item pointing at a deleted product. Postgres's foreign keys and ACID transactions are exactly what make those corrupt half-states impossible.

chunks.title: Prisma
chunks.text: The translator between your code's objects and the database's rows. Prisma lets the backend read and write the database using normal typed objects instead of hand-written SQL — and keeps the schema and code in lock-step. Code thinks in *objects* (order.total); databases think in *tables and SQL*. An ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) is the translator between the two. Prisma is the ORM your backend uses. It starts from one file, schema.prisma, that describes every table in a clean, readable syntax. Run prisma generate and Prisma produces a fully typed client: code that knows your tables exactly, so prisma.order.create({...}) is checked against the real shape of the Order table, with autocomplete and red squiggles for mistakes. Prisma also manages migrations — versioned, repeatable changes to the database's structure — so the schema evolves safely instead of someone editing tables by hand in production. Prisma was chosen because it makes the database type-safe end to end: the same schema.prisma defines the tables *and* generates the types your code uses, so the code literally cannot reference a column that doesn't exist. That kills a whole class of bugs. It also makes everyday data code readable (no string-concatenated SQL), and turns schema changes into reviewable, repeatable migrations rather than risky manual edits. schema.prisma: One file describing every table, field, relation, and index — the single source of truth for data shape. prisma generate: Reads the schema and emits a typed client your TypeScript code imports. The Client: prisma.order.findMany(...) etc. — typed methods for every table. Migrations: Versioned SQL changes that bring any database up to the current schema, repeatably. Raw SQL: Maximum control and speed; you hand-write and hand-maintain every query and lose compile-time safety. TypeORM / Sequelize: Older ORMs; capable but historically clunkier types and rougher migrations than Prisma. Drizzle: A newer, lighter, SQL-flavoured type-safe alternative; smaller ecosystem.

chunks.title: Prisma — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: schema.prisma defines every table; the backend's build runs prisma generate before compiling so the typed client is always in sync. Services call the client (e.g. to create an order and its items inside a transaction), and Prisma turns those calls into the right SQL against Postgres. Because the client's types come from the schema, the rest of the TypeScript codebase inherits exact knowledge of every table — the link described in the TypeScript page. Skip migrations and just edit the live database by hand. Now the database has a column the code doesn't expect (or is missing one the code needs), and the two have silently drifted apart — the next deploy crashes on the first query. Prisma migrations keep code and schema moving together as one reviewed, repeatable step (Part 10).

chunks.title: HTTP & REST
chunks.text: The grammar the app and backend use to talk to each other. HTTP is the request-and-reply language of the web; REST is the tidy convention your backend follows for naming and shaping those requests. HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is how two computers on the web have a conversation. It's strictly request-and-reply: the app sends a request (‘please give me the menu'), the backend sends back a response (‘here it is, and it went fine'). Nothing is pushed unasked; the app always initiates. Every request has a method — the verb. GET means ‘read me something' (and changes nothing); POST means ‘here's something new, create it'; PUT/PATCH update; DELETE removes. It also has a URL (what you're talking about) and a status code in the reply: 200 OK, 404 not found, 401 not logged in, 500 the server broke. REST isn't a technology — it's a widely-followed *convention* for organising an HTTP API around ‘resources' (things like orders and products), addressed by tidy URLs, acted on with the standard methods. Your backend is RESTful: the menu lives at GET /api/v1/menu, an order is created with POST /api/v1/orders. HTTP is simply *the* language of the web — universal, cacheable, understood by every tool, proxy, and browser. Following REST on top of it makes the API predictable: once you know one resource works as GET/POST /api/v1/<thing>, you can guess the rest. The GET-changes-nothing rule is quietly important: it means reads can be safely cached and retried, which is what later lets caching and CDNs speed the whole system up. Method (verb): GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE removes. GET must never change anything. URL / path: Which resource you mean: /api/v1/menu, /api/v1/orders/123. Headers: Metadata travelling with the request — the auth cookie, the CSRF token, the content type. Status code: The reply's verdict: 200 OK, 401 unauthorised, 404 missing, 500 server error. GraphQL: One flexible endpoint where the client asks for exactly the fields it wants; more power, more setup than REST. gRPC: A fast binary protocol for service-to-service calls; great internally, less friendly for public/browser APIs. WebSockets / SSE: For the server *pushing* updates (live order status) rather than the app always asking — see Live sync.

chunks.title: HTTP & REST — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The app's repositories make HTTP requests through the Dio client to RESTful routes under /api/v1. Express maps each method+URL to a handler; the response comes back as JSON with a status code the app reacts to (200 → show the data, 401 → send the user to log in). The v1 in the path is API versioning — it lets a v2 exist later without breaking apps still speaking v1 (Part 09). Break the convention — make a GET that secretly changes data — and you've planted a landmine: caches and link-prefetchers fire GETs freely, so something could ‘place an order' just by a page being previewed. Keeping verbs honest (reads read, writes write) is what makes the whole web's caching and retry machinery safe to use.

chunks.title: JSON
chunks.text: The simple text shape that data travels in between every part of the system. JSON is a lightweight, human-readable way to write down structured data as text — the lingua franca the app, backend and database all understand. When the backend sends the menu to the app, it can't send a living Dart or JavaScript object down a wire — it has to send *text*. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the agreed text format for that: curly braces for objects, square brackets for lists, "key": value pairs inside. It maps onto exactly the things every language already has — objects/maps, arrays/lists, strings, numbers, booleans, null — so both sides can convert effortlessly. The backend turns an object *into* JSON text (‘serialise'); the app turns that text back *into* an object (‘parse'/‘deserialise'). It's readable by humans too, which makes debugging an API a matter of just looking at the response. JSON won because it's *simple* and *universal*: tiny to learn, native to JavaScript, and supported everywhere from Dart to Postgres. For an API that connects a Flutter app, a Node backend, and a Next admin, having one shared data shape they all speak removes a whole category of translation bugs. It's also flexible — new fields can be added to a response without breaking older clients that simply ignore them, which helps the API evolve. Objects { }: Named fields: { "total": 358, "status": "PLACED" } — like a record. Arrays [ ]: Ordered lists: [ "Burger", "Fries" ] — like the items in an order. Primitives: Strings, numbers, booleans, null — the basic values that fill the fields. Serialise / parse: Turning an object into JSON text, and JSON text back into an object. XML: The older, far more verbose markup; powerful but heavy. JSON replaced it for most web APIs. Protocol Buffers: A compact binary format — smaller and faster, but not human-readable and needs a schema on both sides. Form-encoding: Fine for simple HTML form posts; clumsy for the nested data an order needs.

chunks.title: JSON — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Backend handlers reply with res.json(...), turning a JavaScript object into JSON text. The app's repository receives that text and parses it into typed Dart objects like MenuProduct. The app's order request travels *to* the backend as JSON too. Postgres can even store JSON directly — your schema uses Json? columns (e.g. loyalty tier config) for data whose shape is flexible. Let the two sides disagree on the shape — the backend renames total to grand_total in its JSON but the app still reads total — and the app parses null, then renders ‘₹null' or crashes. JSON has no built-in contract enforcement, which is exactly why typed models (Dart classes, TypeScript types from Prisma) sit on top of it to catch a mismatched shape.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Auth — JWT, cookies & CSRF
chunks.title: Auth — JWT, cookies & CSRF
chunks.text: How the system proves who you are — safely — on every request. Auth is two questions answered on every request: who are you (a signed token in an httpOnly cookie), and is this request genuine (a CSRF token). ‘Auth' covers two related jobs. Authentication is proving *who you are* (you log in). Authorisation is deciding *what you're allowed to do* (only an admin can change prices). The web is stateless — each request arrives cold — so you must prove yourself on *every* request, not just once. Your system does this with a JWT (JSON Web Token): a compact, signed badge the backend issues at login that says ‘this is user X'. Signed means it's stamped with a secret only the server knows, so it can't be forged or edited. The token is stored in an httpOnly cookie — a cookie that JavaScript on the page *cannot read* — so even a malicious injected script can't steal your login. Cookies are sent automatically by the browser, which is convenient but opens one hole: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery), where another website quietly fires a request to your backend riding your cookie. The fix is a CSRF token: a separate value the real app reads and echoes back in a header, which a foreign site can't obtain. The popular shortcut is to keep the login token in localStorage and attach it by hand. It's easy — but *any* script that runs on your page can read localStorage and walk off with the login. The httpOnly cookie removes that entire class of theft. The price is CSRF risk, which the CSRF token closes. Every security choice is a trade; this stack picks the safer pair. Signed JWTs also keep the backend stateless — your identity rides in the token, so no server has to ‘remember' your session, which is what lets the backend run many copies (Part 09). JWT: A signed token carrying ‘who you are', tamper-proof because only the server holds the signing secret. httpOnly cookie: Where the token lives. JavaScript can't read it, so a page script can't steal the login. CSRF token: A second value the genuine app echoes back, proving the request came from the real app, not a forger. Authorisation checks: requireAdmin and friends — deciding what a proven identity is allowed to do. Token in localStorage: Simple, but readable by any script on the page — a real XSS theft risk this stack deliberately avoids. Server-side sessions: The server stores each session; simple and revocable, but stateful, which complicates horizontal scaling. OAuth / ‘Sign in with…': Delegate identity to Google/Apple; great UX, an extra integration and dependency.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Auth — JWT, cookies & CSRF
chunks.title: Auth — JWT, cookies & CSRF — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: On login the backend sets an httpOnly cookie holding a signed JWT. State-changing requests must also carry a matching CSRF token. Middleware enforces both: requireAdmin checks you're a logged-in admin, requireCsrf checks the request is genuine, before any handler runs. The admin panel reuses exactly this for every write, which is why changing a price is safe (Part 04, Part 06). Drop the CSRF check and stay logged in as admin. Now you visit a booby-trapped page that silently POSTs to your admin API; the browser helpfully attaches your cookie, the backend sees a ‘valid' admin request, and prices change or data is deleted under your own login. Or store the JWT in localStorage instead of an httpOnly cookie, and one injected script steals it outright. The cookie-plus-CSRF pairing is precisely what closes both doors.

chunks.title: Idempotency
chunks.text: Why doing the same thing twice has the same effect as doing it once. An idempotent operation can be repeated safely — a retried ‘place order' charges you once, not twice, because the system recognises the repeat. Networks are unreliable. The app sends ‘place order', the reply gets lost on the way back, so the app retries — but the backend may have *already* processed the first one. Without protection, you'd be charged twice and get two orders. Idempotency is the property that makes a repeated request land exactly once. The mechanism is an idempotency key: a unique token the client attaches to an attempt. The backend records keys it has seen. The first request with a given key does the work; any later request with the *same* key is recognised as a duplicate and quietly returns the original result instead of repeating the action. In your schema this is enforced at the strongest possible level — the database. The Order table's idempotency_key is marked unique, so a duplicate insert physically cannot happen; the second one bounces off a wall. Anything touching money *must* survive retries, and retries are not optional — phones drop signal mid-request constantly. Idempotency is the cheapest, most reliable way to make ‘exactly once' true in a world that only really offers ‘at least once'. Putting the guarantee in the database (a unique key) rather than just in code means even two requests racing at the very same instant can't both win — the database serialises them. Idempotency key: A unique token per attempt, like earn:order:<id> or a UUID the client generates. Unique constraint: The database refuses a second row with the same key — the hard, last line of defence. Safe verbs: GET, PUT and DELETE are naturally idempotent; POST (create) is the one that needs a key. Return the original: On a duplicate, hand back the first result rather than erroring or redoing. Hope it doesn't happen: Works until the first dropped connection; then it's a double charge and an angry customer. Check-then-insert in code: ‘Does this order exist? No → create it' — but two racing requests can both pass the check. A unique constraint can't be raced. A distributed lock: Lock the operation so only one runs; heavier machinery, useful when there's no natural unique key.

chunks.title: Idempotency — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The Order table has a unique idempotency_key, so a retried checkout can't create a second order. Loyalty goes further: each LoyaltyTransaction carries a key like earn:order:<id>, guaranteeing an order credits points exactly once even if processed twice. You can feel this directly in the Loyalty-ledger simulator: hit ‘Retry last order' and watch the credit be refused. Remove the key and let a flaky network retry a payment. The customer is charged twice, two identical orders hit the kitchen, and the loyalty points are doubled — all from one tap that simply got retried. The single unique column is what turns that disaster into a non-event.

chunks.title: Transactions & ACID
chunks.text: All-or-nothing writes — the bedrock of never losing money or orders. A transaction groups several database writes so they all succeed together or all undo together — there's no half-finished state. Placing an order isn't one write — it's several: the Order row, its OrderItem rows, the OrderPayment. If the server crashed after writing the payment but before the order, you'd have a charge for an order that doesn't exist. A transaction prevents that by wrapping the writes so they happen all-or-nothing: if any step fails, every step is rolled back and the database looks as if nothing happened. Databases like Postgres guarantee transactions are ACID: Atomic (all-or-nothing), Consistent (rules are never left broken), Isolated (concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work), Durable (once committed, it survives a crash). Those four letters are why a relational database is trusted with money. The moment a system involves money or linked records, partial writes are unacceptable — they create charges without orders, points without purchases, items without parents. Transactions are the standard, decades-proven way to make multi-step writes safe. They pair with idempotency: idempotency stops the *same* write happening twice; transactions stop a *group* of writes happening halfway. Begin / commit / rollback: Start a transaction, then either commit all of it or roll all of it back. Atomicity: All the writes land, or none do. No half-orders. Isolation: Concurrent transactions don't see each other's unfinished work. Durability: Once committed, it's permanent — it survives a power cut a millisecond later. Separate writes + cleanup jobs: Write each step alone and run a background job to fix inconsistencies; fragile and always racing reality. Sagas (across services): When data spans many services with no shared transaction, you coordinate with compensating undo-steps. Powerful, much more complex. Just don't: Skip them for speed and inherit a database full of impossible half-states. Never worth it for money.

chunks.title: Transactions & ACID — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Order placement wraps the Order, its OrderItems, and the OrderPayment in one Prisma transaction, so a failure anywhere undoes the whole thing — there is no charge without an order, ever. Loyalty earn/spend is written transactionally too, keeping the account balance and its ledger row consistent. This is the guarantee dramatised in the order-journey simulator and Part 05. Write the steps one by one with no transaction, then have the server hiccup mid-way. Now the payment exists but the order doesn't (a charge for nothing) — or the order exists but the payment doesn't (free food). At scale, isolation failures also let two transactions corrupt each other's half-done work. ACID transactions make every one of those half-states impossible.

chunks.title: Ledgers
chunks.text: Track points and money like a bank: never a bare balance, always a tape of movements. A ledger records every change as its own immutable row, so the balance is the running total of a history you can always audit. The naïve way to track loyalty points is a single number you add to and subtract from. The problem: when it's wrong, you have no idea *how* it got wrong, can't prove what a customer earned, and can't undo one bad change. A ledger fixes this by storing every movement as its own row — a signed amount, a reason, a timestamp — and treating the balance as the *sum of the tape*, not a standalone figure. Crucially the ledger is append-only: you never edit or delete a row, you only add new ones (including a reversal row to ‘undo' an earlier one). That immutability is what makes it trustworthy — the history can't be quietly rewritten. Your LoyaltyTransaction table is a textbook ledger: a type (EARN/REDEEM/ADJUST/REVERSAL/EXPIRE), a signed points, a balance_after snapshot for auditing, a source, and an idempotency_key. Anything people care about losing — money, points, inventory — converges on this design, because it's the only one that answers ‘what happened?' Disputes become readable, mistakes become reversible (by appending, not editing), and double-credits are blocked by an idempotency key on each row. It also pairs with optimistic concurrency: the account carries a version counter, so two requests trying to spend the same points can't both win — the second notices the version moved and backs off. Append-only rows: Every earn/redeem is a new immutable entry; nothing is edited or deleted. Signed amounts: +20 earned, -30 redeemed — the direction is in the number. balance_after: A snapshot of the running total at each row, so any point in history is auditable. Reversals: To undo, you append an opposite entry — the original stays as a record. A bare balance number: Smaller and simpler — until it's wrong, and then it's unexplainable and unfixable. Balance + an audit log on the side: Better, but the two can drift; in a true ledger the balance *is* the log, so they can't disagree. Event sourcing (whole system): The same idea applied to everything, not just money — maximal auditability, much more machinery.

chunks.title: Ledgers — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: LoyaltyTransaction is the append-only ledger; LoyaltyAccount holds the derived points_balance plus a version for safe concurrent spends and lifetime_points that only ever rises (it drives tiers). Earning and redeeming append signed rows with a balance_after snapshot and an idempotency key. The Loyalty-ledger simulator lets you watch the tape grow and try (and fail) to double-credit. Keep only a balance and let a bug subtract 30 points twice. The number is now wrong by 30 and there is no record of why, no way to prove the customer's real balance, and no clean way to reverse exactly one bad change. A ledger turns that into a single reversal row appended to an intact history.

chunks.title: Dio
chunks.text: The app's one network client — every request to the backend goes through it. Dio is the HTTP client the Flutter app uses; configured once with a base URL and interceptors that run on every single request. The app needs to make HTTP requests — fetch the menu, post an order. Dio is the popular Dart library it uses to do that. Rather than each screen writing its own raw network call, the app builds one configured Dio client and shares it everywhere (as apiClientProvider). Dio's killer feature is interceptors: small pieces of code that run automatically on every request and every response. They're the perfect place for cross-cutting concerns — attaching the auth cookie, adding a request-id for tracing, logging, and retrying on a transient blip — so no screen has to remember to do any of it. Because there's a single client, changing how *all* networking behaves (a new base URL, a new header, a retry policy) is a one-place edit. Centralising networking is the same ‘one source of truth' instinct applied to requests: it kills duplicated call-sites and the bugs that come from them (one screen forgets the auth header, another doesn't retry). Interceptors make auth, tracing, and resilience automatic and uniform. It pairs with the repository pattern: screens ask a repository, the repository uses the shared Dio client, and interceptors handle the invisible plumbing. The client: One configured instance with the base URL, shared via apiClientProvider. Interceptors: Run on every request/response: attach auth, add a request-id, log, retry. Base options: Defaults like the backend URL and timeouts, set once for all calls. Error handling: A central place to turn a failed response into a clean, typed error for the UI. http (the basic package): Dart's simple client; fine for a few calls, but no interceptors — you'd hand-roll auth/retry everywhere. Chopper / Retrofit: Code-generated typed API clients built on top of Dio/http; more structure, more build tooling. Raw HttpClient: The lowest level; maximum control, maximum boilerplate.

chunks.title: Dio — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: apiClientProvider builds the shared Dio client; interceptors attach the auth cookie and a request-id and handle logging/retries. Repositories take that client (dependency injection) and make their calls through it — no screen ever touches raw networking. The request-id added here is what lets one order be traced across the backend later (observability, Part 09). Skip the shared client and let every screen call the network directly. The day you change how auth works or add a retry, you're editing dozens of scattered call-sites and missing some — and a momentary network blip with no retry shows a broken screen for a request that would've succeeded half a second later. One client with interceptors fixes all of it in one place.

chunks.title: Next.js & React
chunks.text: The framework behind the admin panel — and this very learning site. React builds web UIs from components; Next.js is the full framework around React that adds routing, server rendering, and a build system. React is a library for building web interfaces out of components — reusable pieces of UI (a button, a table, a form) that describe themselves from data, just like Flutter widgets. You compose small components into pages. Next.js is the framework *around* React that turns it into a complete app: file-based routing (a file at app/users/page.tsx becomes the /users route), server rendering (pages can be built on the server for speed and SEO), a build system, and an API layer. The admin panel is a Next.js app; so is this site you're reading. A key Next idea is server vs client components: most of a page can render on the server (fast, no JavaScript shipped), and only the genuinely interactive bits run in the browser. This very page is mostly server-rendered; the sidebar and simulators are client components. For an admin panel you want fast pages, real routing, and easy data-loading without hand-building a server — exactly Next.js's sweet spot. React's component model also makes a consistent, reusable UI library straightforward. Server components mean less JavaScript shipped to the browser, so pages load fast and feel snappy — which is why this learning site renders its dense reading pages on the server and only hydrates the interactive widgets. Components: Reusable UI pieces that render from props/state — React's core unit. File-based routing: app/<path>/page.tsx becomes a route automatically. Server vs client: Server components render on the server (fast); client components ("use client") run in the browser for interactivity. Build & render modes: Static, server-rendered, or hybrid — chosen per page for speed. Plain React (Vite): Just the library + a bundler; you add routing and rendering yourself. Lighter, less batteries-included. Vue / Nuxt, Svelte / SvelteKit: Rival component frameworks with their own full-stack kits; similar ideas, different syntax. Angular: A heavier, all-in-one framework; more opinionated and verbose than React.

chunks.title: Next.js & React — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The admin panel is a Next.js app: each admin screen is a route under app/, built from React components, talking to the backend's API. Refine sits on top to generate the CRUD screens. This learning site is Next.js too — server-rendered reading pages plus client components for the sidebar, roadmap, and simulators. The mobile app uses Flutter, not React — but the *idea* (compose UI from small components/widgets) is the same on both sides. Render everything as heavy client-side JavaScript (the old single-page-app default) and the admin's first load gets slow and blank until a big bundle downloads and runs. Next.js's server rendering sends a ready-made page first, so it's useful immediately — and ships less JavaScript by keeping non-interactive parts on the server.

chunks.title: Refine
chunks.text: Generates the admin's CRUD screens so they don't have to be hand-built. Refine is a React framework that turns ‘here are my resources and how to fetch them' into ready-made list, create, edit, and detail screens. An admin console is mostly the same four screens repeated for every kind of thing: a list of items, a create form, an edit form, and a detail view. Developers call this ‘CRUD' — Create, Read, Update, Delete. Hand-coding hundreds of nearly-identical forms is tedious and error-prone. Refine is a React framework that *generates* this scaffolding. You declare your resources (products, stores, users) and give it providers — a data provider that knows how to talk to your backend's API, and an auth provider that knows how to log in — and Refine wires up consistent CRUD screens, pagination, forms, and routing on top. It runs inside Next.js, so you get Refine's productivity *and* Next's routing and rendering. Refine was chosen to get a real, consistent admin console *fast* without hand-coding repetitive forms. Because every resource flows through the same data and auth providers, behaviour (and security) is uniform across the whole panel. It's also flexible: where a screen needs something bespoke, you drop down to plain React/Next — so you're never boxed in by the generator. Resources: The things you administer — products, stores, users — declared once. Data provider: The adapter that tells Refine how to read/write your backend's API. Auth provider: How login, logout, and ‘who am I' work — wired to the cookie+CSRF auth. Generated CRUD: List, create, edit, show screens with forms, tables, and pagination, ready-made. Build screens by hand: Total control; enormous repetition and the bugs that come with copy-paste forms. React-Admin: The most established CRUD framework; similar idea, different conventions and ecosystem. A hosted admin (Retool, etc.): Fastest to start, but your admin lives in someone else's tool and pricing.

chunks.title: Refine — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The admin panel declares resources (stores, users, catalogue, content) and a data provider pointing at the backend's /api/v1 admin routes, plus an auth provider using the httpOnly cookie + CSRF flow. Refine then renders the list/create/edit/show screens staff use to run the business. Those writes land in the same database the customer app reads — the live-control trick of Part 06. Hand-build forty bespoke CRUD screens and watch them drift: this list paginates, that one doesn't; this form validates, that one forgets; one screen skips the CSRF header and quietly breaks. A single framework with shared data/auth providers keeps every screen consistent — and consistently secure.

chunks.title: SQL & indexes
chunks.text: The language for asking the database questions — and the trick that keeps answers instant. SQL is how you query a relational database; an index is the pre-sorted lookup that makes those queries fast even over millions of rows. SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language for talking to a relational database like Postgres. You *describe what you want* and the database figures out how to get it: SELECT * FROM "Order" WHERE store_id = '...' AND status = 'PLACED' means ‘give me this store's placed orders'. JOIN stitches linked tables together (an order with its items); INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE change data. By default, finding rows means scanning the whole table — fine for a hundred rows, ruinous for ten million. An index is a pre-sorted structure (think the index at the back of a book) that lets the database jump straight to matching rows instead of reading every page. You usually don't hand-write this SQL — Prisma generates it from your code — but knowing what's happening underneath is what lets you reason about speed. SQL is declarative — you say *what*, not *how* — so the database's query planner can pick the fastest path, use indexes, and adapt as data grows, without you rewriting queries. It's a decades-proven, universal language for exactly this. Indexes are the single biggest lever for query speed. Your schema adds them deliberately on the columns real queries filter by, so the app stays fast as the orders table grows. SELECT … WHERE: Read rows that match a condition — the everyday query. JOIN: Combine linked tables: an order together with its items and user. INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE: The writes — create, change, remove rows. Indexes: Pre-sorted lookups on chosen columns that turn a full scan into a jump. NoSQL query styles: Document/key-value stores use their own query models; great for some shapes, weaker at ad-hoc joins SQL does easily. Raw scans / in-app filtering: Pull everything and filter in code — fine for tiny data, catastrophic at scale. Hand-tuned SQL vs an ORM: Raw SQL gives control; Prisma generates safe SQL for you. Most apps mix: ORM for the 95%, raw SQL for the hot 5%.

chunks.title: SQL & indexes — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Prisma turns code like prisma.order.findMany({ where: { store_id, status } }) into SQL against Postgres. The schema declares indexes — e.g. @@index([store_id, status]) on Order and @@index([account_id, created_at]) on the loyalty ledger — so the queries that matter stay instant. That ‘this store's pending orders' lookup the admin runs constantly is fast precisely because of that composite index. Drop the indexes and the queries still *work* — they just get slower every day as data grows, until ‘show this store's orders' takes seconds and the admin grinds to a halt under load. Worse, missing indexes often look fine in testing (small data) and only bite in production. Adding the right index turns a full-table scan back into an instant jump.

chunks.title: Live sync (SSE)
chunks.text: How an admin's change shows up on screens without anyone hitting refresh. Server-Sent Events let the backend push a little ‘something changed' nudge to connected clients, so the UI updates live. Normally the app only learns things by *asking* (an HTTP request). But sometimes the server needs to tell clients ‘something just changed' — an admin updated the menu, an order's status advanced. Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a simple way to do that: the client opens one long-lived connection and the server *pushes* small event messages down it whenever there's news.
