It's one-directional (server → client) and rides ordinary HTTP, which makes it lightweight and easy compared to a full two-way WebSocket. Perfect for ‘broadcast a nudge', not for chat. Your backend has a sync.service that broadcasts these events; clients listening on the stream react — typically by re-fetching the now-changed data. For admin-driven content, ‘change it and it's live' is the whole promise — and waiting for the next poll, or asking the user to refresh, breaks the magic. SSE delivers near-instant updates with far less complexity than WebSockets, and reuses your existing HTTP/auth. It keeps the model simple: the server still owns the truth and just *signals* change; clients re-read through the same API they always use, so there's no second source of data to keep consistent. The event stream: One long-lived HTTP connection the server keeps open to push messages. Events: Small typed messages — ‘menu changed', ‘config changed' — broadcast to listeners. The sync service: Backend code that decides what changed and pushes the nudge. Client reaction: On an event, the client re-fetches the affected data and the UI updates live. Polling: Ask every N seconds. Dead simple, but laggy and wasteful — lots of ‘nothing changed' requests. WebSockets: Full two-way real-time channel; more powerful (chat, live cursors) and more to operate. Overkill for one-way nudges. Push notifications: For reaching a closed app on the device; a different tool than in-app live updates.

chunks.title: Live sync (SSE) — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The backend's sync.service broadcasts change events over an SSE stream set up in app.ts. When an admin edits content or config, connected clients get a nudge and re-fetch — so the change appears live without a manual refresh. This is the real-time half of the admin story (Part 06): the admin writes, a sync event fires, and screens update themselves. Without live sync you're back to polling or manual refresh: an admin drops a price, but customers keep seeing the old menu until their app happens to re-fetch — and the ‘instant control' promise quietly dies. (You must still invalidate caches on change, or even a re-fetch returns the stale value — see Caching.)

chunks.title: State machines
chunks.text: An order is always in exactly one known state, and only some moves are legal. A state machine restricts a thing to a fixed set of states and only the allowed transitions between them — so ‘impossible' situations can't occur. Some things move through a defined lifecycle. An order is PENDING_PAYMENT, then PLACED, PREPARING, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, COMPLETED — or CANCELLED. A state machine models exactly this: a fixed list of states, and a fixed list of allowed transitions between them. The power is in what it *forbids*. An order can't jump from DELIVERED back to PREPARING, and it's never in two states at once or some vague in-between. By only permitting legal moves, a whole category of corrupt situations becomes impossible by design. Your OrderStatus is precisely this set of states, and every move is recorded in an append-only OrderEvent log stamped with who made it. Modelling a lifecycle as explicit states + legal transitions prevents the messy ‘flag soup' alternative (a pile of booleans like isPaid, isShipped that can contradict each other). With one state field, the order is never in a contradictory condition. The transition log doubles as an audit trail: you can replay an order's entire history and know exactly who moved it, when — invaluable for disputes and debugging. States: The fixed set a thing can be in: the OrderStatus values. Transitions: The allowed moves between states; everything else is rejected. Events / triggers: What causes a move — payment confirmed, kitchen done, driver delivered. History log: An append-only record (OrderEvent) of every transition and who caused it. Boolean flags: isPaid, isDelivered… — they can combine into impossible states (delivered but not paid). The bug source a state machine removes. A status string with no rules: One field, but any value can be set to any other — you lose the ‘only legal moves' guarantee. Workflow engines: For very complex, long-running processes you might use a dedicated engine; overkill for an order's handful of states.

chunks.title: State machines — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: OrderStatus is the enum of states; transitions advance an order along its lifecycle, and each move appends an OrderEvent with an actor (customer / admin / system / pos). That log is the order's auditable history. The order-journey simulator walks these states; Part 08 covers them in depth. Replace the state machine with loose booleans and you'll eventually produce an order that's delivered but not paid, or cancelled yet still preparing — contradictions no one intended and everyone has to clean up. One state field with enforced transitions makes those contradictions unrepresentable.

chunks.title: Caching
chunks.text: Compute the answer once, serve it many times — and the hard part: knowing when it's stale. A cache keeps a ready-made copy of a costly-to-produce answer (like the menu) so most requests are served instantly instead of recomputed. Some answers are expensive to produce and rarely change — the menu, for instance, is read constantly but edited occasionally. Caching means keeping a ready copy of that answer close by, so the vast majority of requests are served from the copy instead of hitting the database every time. Caches live at several layers: in the backend's memory, in a shared fast store like Redis that all backend copies share, and — for images and assets — in a CDN, a network of servers near your customers around the world. The genuinely hard part isn't *storing* the cache, it's invalidation: knowing when the cached copy is out of date and must be thrown away. ‘There are only two hard things in computer science: naming things, and cache invalidation.' Caching is the highest-leverage speed-and-cost win available: it turns repeated expensive work into a single computation served thousands of times, slashing both latency and database load. For read-heavy data like a menu, it's transformational. But it's added *deliberately and late* (Part 09), because every cache introduces the risk of serving stale data — so you only take that on when a real measurement says you need the speed. In-memory cache: Fastest, lives inside one backend process; lost on restart and not shared. Shared cache (Redis): A fast store all backend copies read, so they agree on the cached value. CDN: Caches images/assets on servers near the user for instant, global delivery. Invalidation: Throwing away a stale copy when the underlying data changes — the hard part. No cache: Always fresh, never stale — but every read pays full price. Right until traffic makes it too slow. Short time-to-live (TTL): Auto-expire cached copies after N seconds; simple, but accepts up to N seconds of staleness. Explicit invalidation: Drop the cache the instant data changes; freshest, but you must wire every change to its invalidation.

chunks.title: Caching — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The menu and config are the natural cache candidates — read constantly, changed occasionally from the admin. The discipline that makes it safe: when an admin edits a price (Part 06), the cached menu must be invalidated so the next read recomputes the fresh value, and a live-sync event nudges clients to re-fetch. This is a scale layer (Part 09): added around an already-correct design, not baked in from day one. Cache the menu but forget to invalidate it. An admin drops a price; the cache keeps cheerfully serving the old one for hours; customers see — and pay — last week's price. Stale caches are subtle because everything *looks* fast and fine. Wiring every change to its invalidation is what keeps ‘fast' from quietly becoming ‘wrong'.

chunks.title: Concurrency & races
chunks.text: What happens when two requests touch the same thing at the same instant. Concurrency is many things happening at once; a race condition is the bug where two of them collide on the same data and corrupt it. A backend serves many users at the same time — that's concurrency, and it's essential for performance. The danger is the race condition: two requests read the same value, both act on it, and one silently clobbers the other. Classic example: an account has 100 points; two ‘spend 80' requests both read 100, both think there's enough, and both succeed — now the balance is -60. The fixes share one idea: make the conflicting step *atomic* (indivisible). Optimistic concurrency adds a version number to a row; you only write if the version is unchanged since you read it, so the second writer notices someone moved first and retries. Conditional updates push the check into the database (‘subtract 80 *only if* balance ≥ 80'). Locks make others wait. The database, being the single serialisation point, is where these guarantees are made. On anything shared and valuable — points, stock, balances — races aren't rare edge cases; under real traffic they happen constantly. Handling them is the difference between a balance you can trust and one that mysteriously goes negative. Optimistic concurrency is preferred here because conflicts are *rare*: you don't pay the cost of locking on every request, you just detect the occasional collision and retry. It keeps the common path fast. Race condition: Two operations interleave on the same data and produce a wrong result. Optimistic concurrency: A version column; write only if it hasn't changed since you read — else retry. Conditional update: Push the check into the write itself: ‘decrement only if ≥ amount'. Locks: Make one operation wait for another to finish; safe, but can slow things down. Ignore it: Works in testing (one user at a time); breaks in production the first time two requests collide. Pessimistic locks: Lock the row before reading so no one else can touch it. Always-safe, but slower and can deadlock. Single-threaded queue: Funnel conflicting operations through one worker so they can't overlap. Simple, limits throughput.

chunks.title: Concurrency & races — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The LoyaltyAccount carries a version counter for optimistic concurrency, and the balance is kept >= 0 by conditional updates — so two requests trying to spend the same points can't both win; the second is rejected and the balance never goes negative. Idempotency keys handle the related ‘same request twice' problem. These guarantees ultimately rest on the database serialising writes — the same backbone that powers transactions. Ignore concurrency and let two ‘redeem points' requests land together. Both read the old balance, both pass the ‘enough points?' check, both write — and the customer spends points they didn't have, or a discount applies twice. A version check or conditional update makes the second one notice the collision and fail cleanly, so value is never conjured from a race.

chunks.title: Docker & containers
chunks.text: Pack an app and everything it needs into one sealed box that runs identically everywhere. A container is your app plus its exact environment, frozen into an image that runs the same on your laptop, a teammate's, and production. 'Works on my machine' fails because your laptop isn't the server — different OS, library versions, settings. A container fixes this by bundling your app together with the exact runtime, libraries, and config it needs into one image that runs identically anywhere a container engine exists. Docker is the tool that builds these images (from a Dockerfile recipe) and runs them as containers. Unlike a full virtual machine, a container shares the host's OS kernel, so it's tiny and starts in milliseconds, not minutes. Containers make the environment part of the artifact, so the thing you tested is byte-for-byte the thing that runs in production — killing a whole class of 'it worked locally' bugs. They're also the unit that orchestrators like Kubernetes schedule and scale. Versus a full VM: containers share the host kernel, so they're far lighter (MBs not GBs) and start instantly — you can run dozens on one machine. Image: A frozen, read-only snapshot of your app + its environment, built in layers. Dockerfile: The recipe: base image, copy code, install deps, the start command. Container: A running instance of an image — isolated, disposable, fast to start. Registry: Where images are stored & shared (Docker Hub, GHCR) so prod pulls the exact image you built. Virtual machines: Stronger isolation (own kernel) but heavy and slow to boot; containers are the modern default for app packaging. Buildpacks / Nixpacks: Auto-detect and build an image with no hand-written Dockerfile — convenient, less control. Deploy raw source: Let the host install deps at deploy time — simple, but reintroduces 'works on my machine' drift.

chunks.title: Docker & containers — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Bake a secret or a host-specific path into an image and it leaks or breaks elsewhere. Forget to pin versions in your Dockerfile and a rebuild months later silently pulls newer, incompatible deps — the image is no longer reproducible. Treat images as immutable, version-pinned, and secret-free, and inject config via environment variables at run time.

chunks.title: CI/CD
chunks.text: Automatically test every change and ship it — so broken code is caught before users see it, and releasing is boring. CI runs your tests on every push; CD deploys what passed — turning 'release day' into a non-event that happens many times a day. CI (Continuous Integration) means every code change is automatically built and tested the moment it's pushed, so problems surface in minutes — not weeks later when everything's tangled together. CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment) takes the changes that passed and automatically ships them to staging or production. Concretely it's a pipeline — a sequence of steps (install → lint → test → build → deploy) defined in a file (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI) that runs on a fresh machine for every push or pull request. The longer a bug lives, the more expensive it is. CI catches it within minutes of being written, when it's cheap to fix and the author still remembers the change. CD makes releases small and frequent, so each is low-risk and easy to roll back — the opposite of a scary quarterly 'big bang'. It also removes humans from the repetitive, error-prone parts (running tests, building, deploying), so those happen the same way every time. Trigger: What starts the pipeline — a push, a pull request, a tag, a schedule. Stages / jobs: install → lint → test → build → deploy, each able to fail the run. Runner: A fresh, clean machine that executes the steps — reproducible every time. Gates & environments: 'Tests must pass to merge', and promotion staging → prod. Manual testing + deploys: Works at tiny scale; becomes a bottleneck and a 'forgot to run the tests' incident source as the team grows. Continuous Delivery (vs Deployment): Auto-deploy to staging but require a human click for production — a common, safe middle ground.

chunks.title: CI/CD — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: A flaky or slow test suite is the silent killer: people start ignoring red builds or skipping CI, and the safety net rots. Deploy without a migration step and code hits a database missing a column. Keep tests fast and reliable, gate merges on green, and make schema changes part of the pipeline.

chunks.title: Observability
chunks.text: Seeing what your running system is actually doing — so you find problems before your users tell you. Logs, metrics, and traces working together to answer 'what's happening, where, and why' in a live system you can't put under a microscope. At ten users you watch the terminal. At a million you can't — you need observability: the ability to ask new questions about a running system from the data it emits. Three pillars: logs (timestamped events: 'order 8f3 failed'), metrics (numbers over time: latency, error rate, requests/sec), and traces (one request's full journey across services). The goal isn't just dashboards — it's answering a question you didn't anticipate ('why are payments slow only in Mumbai after 9pm?') from data you're already collecting. You can't fix what you can't see. Without observability an outage is a frantic guessing game; with it you follow the evidence to the cause in minutes. The pillars complement: metrics say *something*'s wrong, traces say *where*, logs say *what*. It also catches slow degradations (a leak, creeping latency) before they become outages — the difference between proactive and reactive operations. Logs: Discrete timestamped events — best for 'what exactly happened here'. Metrics: Cheap numeric time-series — best for 'is it healthy' and alerting. Traces: One request followed across services via a shared request-id — best for 'where's the slow part'. Alerts & SLOs: Rules that page a human when a metric crosses a user-experience threshold. Just logging: Logs alone are noisy and expensive to search at scale; metrics and traces make the haystack navigable. Monitoring (the older term): Watching known dashboards for known problems; observability adds answering *unknown* questions after the fact.

chunks.title: Observability — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Log everything and you drown in noise and a huge bill; log too little and you're blind during the one incident that matters. No request-id and a trace can't be stitched across services. Alert on everything and people tune out (alert fatigue). The craft is signal over volume: structured logs, alerts tied to user-facing SLOs, and a request-id on every call.

chunks.title: The cloud
chunks.text: Renting someone else's always-on computers — and the managed services on top — instead of owning the hardware. Computers in someone else's data center that you rent by the minute, plus higher-level services (databases, queues, storage) you rent instead of running yourself. A server is a computer that runs all the time to answer requests. The cloud means renting those computers from a provider (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, Vercel) instead of buying and racking your own — paying for what you use, scaling up or down on demand. The real power is the managed services layered on top: instead of installing and babysitting a database, a queue, or a load balancer, you rent one the provider operates, patches, and scales for you. Owning servers means huge upfront cost, capacity you must guess in advance, and a team to run them. The cloud turns that into pay-as-you-go: start tiny, scale instantly for a spike, and never touch hardware. Managed services let a small team run systems that used to need a whole ops department. The trade is cost at very large scale and lock-in to a provider's APIs — which is why some big companies repatriate workloads or stay multi-cloud. Compute: Where code runs: virtual machines, containers, or serverless functions. Storage: Object storage (S3) for files, block storage for disks, plus CDNs near users. Managed data & messaging: Databases, caches, and queues you rent instead of operating. Regions & availability zones: Physical locations; spreading across zones survives a data-center failure. On-premise (own hardware): Full control and predictable cost at huge scale; heavy capital and ops burden. Serverless / PaaS (Vercel, Lambda): Rent at an even higher level — just deploy code; less control, fastest to ship. Hybrid / multi-cloud: Mix owned + rented, or several providers, to balance cost, risk, and lock-in.

chunks.title: The cloud — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Pay-per-use cuts both ways: a misconfigured autoscaler or an infinite loop can run up a massive bill overnight. Putting everything in one availability zone means one data-center outage takes you down. Leaning on provider-specific services deepens lock-in. Guardrails: budgets and alerts, multi-zone deployment, and keeping the truly portable parts portable.

chunks.title: Embeddings & vector search
chunks.text: Turning text (or images) into lists of numbers so a computer can measure meaning by distance. An embedding is a vector — a long list of numbers — that places text in 'meaning space', where similar things sit close together, enabling search by meaning instead of keywords. Computers compare numbers, not meaning. An embedding model converts text into a vector (say, 1,536 numbers) positioned so that texts with similar meaning land near each other in that high-dimensional space. 'dog' and 'puppy' end up close; 'dog' and 'invoice' end up far apart. Once everything is a vector, semantic search is just geometry: embed the query, find the nearest vectors. This is the engine behind search-by-meaning, recommendations, and RAG (feeding an LLM the most relevant documents). Keyword search misses meaning: it can't tell that 'how do I get my money back' matches a doc titled 'Refunds'. Embeddings capture meaning, so search finds the right thing even with different words. They're also the bridge that lets LLMs use *your* private, up-to-date data (RAG) rather than only what they were trained on. Compared to training a custom model, embeddings + search are cheap, fast, and update instantly — just embed new documents and add them. Embedding model: A neural network that maps text → a fixed-length vector capturing meaning. Vector: The list of numbers (the coordinates) for one piece of text. Similarity metric: Cosine similarity / distance — how 'close' two vectors are in meaning. Vector database: A store (pgvector, Pinecone, FAISS) that finds nearest vectors fast at scale. Keyword / TF-IDF search: Fast, transparent, no model needed (this site's assistant uses it) — but blind to synonyms and meaning. Fine-tuning an LLM on your data: Bakes knowledge into the model; expensive and slow to update, vs. embeddings you refresh instantly.

chunks.title: Embeddings & vector search — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Embeddings are only as good as the model and the chunking: split documents badly and the right answer never surfaces. They're also a black box — hard to explain *why* two things were judged similar. And at scale a brute-force nearest-neighbor search is too slow, so you need an approximate vector index (trading a little accuracy for speed). Match the model to your domain, chunk thoughtfully, and measure retrieval quality.

chunks.title: Kubernetes
chunks.text: The manager for many containers — it runs them, heals them, and scales them so you don't babysit servers. Kubernetes keeps the right number of your containers running across a fleet of machines, restarting failures and scaling on demand — you declare the goal, it makes it true. A single container is great, but production needs many copies across many machines, restarted when they crash, replaced on deploy, and scaled with load. Doing that by hand is impossible. Kubernetes (k8s) is the orchestrator that does it for you. You don't tell it *how* — you declare the desired state ('I want 5 replicas of this image, reachable here'), and Kubernetes continuously makes reality match: starting and stopping containers, replacing dead ones, and rolling out new versions without downtime. Kubernetes turns 'operate a fleet of servers' into 'declare what you want'. It self-heals (restarts crashes), scales (adds replicas under load), and deploys without downtime (rolling updates) — capabilities that used to need a large ops team. The same manifests also run on any cloud. The cost is real complexity — it's a powerful, intricate system. For a small app, a simpler platform (Vercel, a single container host) is often the wiser choice until you actually need fleet-scale orchestration. Pod: The smallest unit — one (or a few tightly-coupled) containers that run together. Deployment: Declares 'keep N copies of this version running'; handles rollouts and rollbacks. Service: A stable address that load-balances across the pods behind it. Control loop: Controllers constantly compare desired vs actual state and fix the difference. Managed platforms (Vercel, Render, Fly): Hide orchestration entirely — just deploy; far simpler, less control, great until you outgrow them. Docker Compose / Swarm: Lighter multi-container orchestration for small setups; less powerful than k8s. Serverless: No servers or containers to manage at all — a different model with different limits.

chunks.title: Kubernetes — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Kubernetes' power is a foot-gun: a misconfigured resource limit can starve or OOM-kill your pods, a bad readiness probe can take all traffic down, and the learning curve means small teams drown in YAML. The honest rule: adopt it when you genuinely have many services and a team to run it — not because it's fashionable.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — RAG — grounding an LLM
chunks.title: RAG — grounding an LLM
chunks.text: Give an LLM your own, up-to-date documents to answer from — instead of relying only on what it memorized in training. Retrieval-Augmented Generation: search your documents for the most relevant chunks, hand them to the LLM as context, and have it answer grounded in those real sources. An LLM only knows what it saw in training — it can't know your private docs, and it 'hallucinates' confident wrong answers when it doesn't know. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) fixes this: before answering, you retrieve the most relevant pieces of your own knowledge base and feed them to the model as context, so it answers from real sources. The pipeline: chunk your documents → (often) embed them into vectors → on a question, find the closest chunks → put them into the prompt → the LLM synthesizes a grounded answer. This very site's assistant is a small RAG: it searches an in-repo index and grounds the answer in the matching content. RAG is how you make an LLM useful on *your* data without the cost and staleness of fine-tuning. Update a document and the next answer reflects it instantly — no retraining. It also reduces hallucination (the model has the facts in front of it) and lets you show sources, which builds trust. Versus fine-tuning: RAG keeps knowledge external and fresh; fine-tuning bakes behaviour/style into the model. They solve different problems and are often combined. Chunking: Splitting documents into retrievable pieces — too big and retrieval is fuzzy, too small and context is lost. Retrieval: Finding the most relevant chunks for a query — by keywords (TF-IDF) or meaning (embeddings). Augmentation: Injecting those chunks into the prompt as 'context to answer from'. Generation: The LLM synthesizes a grounded answer, ideally citing its sources. Fine-tuning: Train the model on your data — great for style/format, expensive and slow to update with new facts. Long context (stuff it all in): Paste all docs into the prompt; simple but hits token limits and cost, and dilutes relevance. Plain prompting: Just ask the model; fine for general knowledge, blind to your private/current data.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — RAG — grounding an LLM
chunks.title: RAG — grounding an LLM — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: RAG is only as good as retrieval: if the search returns the wrong chunks, the model confidently answers from the wrong context (garbage in, garbage out). Bad chunking, a weak embedding model, or no relevance filtering all surface as 'it sounds right but it's wrong.' The fixes: measure retrieval quality, chunk thoughtfully, and tell the model to say 'I don't know' when the context is thin.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Rendering — CSR · SSR · SSG · ISR
chunks.title: Rendering — CSR · SSR · SSG · ISR
chunks.text: Where a web page gets built — in the browser, on the server, or ahead of time — and the trade-offs of each. CSR, SSR, SSG, and ISR are four answers to 'who assembles the HTML, and when' — trading off first-paint speed, freshness, and server cost. A web page's HTML has to be built somewhere. The four common strategies: CSR (Client-Side Rendering) — send a near-empty page + JavaScript and let the browser build it; SSR (Server-Side Rendering) — the server builds fresh HTML on each request; SSG (Static Site Generation) — build all pages once at deploy time and serve the files; ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration) — static, but quietly re-built in the background every so often. Modern frameworks like Next.js let you choose per page, because the right answer depends on whether the content is the same for everyone (static) or personalized/changing (server), and how much an instant first paint matters. The choice is about three tensions: first-paint speed (static wins), freshness/personalization (server wins), and cost (static is nearly free; server scales with traffic). Choosing per page lets a marketing page be static and instant while a dashboard is server-rendered and personalized. It also affects SEO: crawlers see full HTML from SSR/SSG immediately, whereas pure CSR can hide content behind JavaScript until it runs. CSR: Browser builds the page from JS. Great for highly-interactive apps; slower first paint, weaker SEO. SSR: Server builds HTML per request. Fresh + good SEO; more server work per visit. SSG: Pages built at deploy, served as static files. Fastest + cheapest; can go stale. ISR: Static, but regenerated in the background on a schedule — fresh-ish without per-request cost. Pick one globally: Simpler mental model, but forces compromises — a static blog and a live dashboard want different things. Streaming / partial hydration: Newer hybrids send HTML progressively and hydrate only the interactive bits — best of both, more complexity.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Rendering — CSR · SSR · SSG · ISR
chunks.title: Rendering — CSR · SSR · SSG · ISR — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Server-render everything and a traffic spike hammers your servers (and your bill) rebuilding the same page millions of times. Statically generate a page that needs to be fresh and users see stale prices. Lean fully on CSR and the first visit is a blank white screen until a big JS bundle loads — bad for slow phones and SEO. Match the strategy to each page's freshness and interactivity needs.

chunks.title: Rate limiting
chunks.text: Capping how fast anyone can hit your API, so no single client can flood it. Rate limiting puts a ceiling on requests per client per window — protecting the system from abuse, runaway bugs, and accidental stampedes. A rate limit is a rule like ‘at most 100 requests per minute from one client'. Go over it and the server replies 429 Too Many Requests and asks you to slow down. It's the bouncer counting how fast people come through the door. Without it, one buggy app stuck in a retry loop — or one attacker — can send thousands of requests a second and starve everyone else, or run up a huge bill. The limit makes load predictable. Limits are keyed by something that identifies the caller: an API key, a user id, or an IP address. Each key gets its own budget. The alternative — trusting clients to be reasonable — fails the moment one isn't. A single retry storm, a scraping bot, or a misconfigured cron job can take the whole service down for everyone. A limit turns ‘outage' into ‘that one client gets throttled'. It also protects cost and fairness: paid tiers get higher budgets, abuse gets a low one, and capacity planning becomes possible because the maximum load per client is known. Fixed window: Count requests per clock minute. Simple, but a burst at the boundary can briefly double the rate. Sliding window: A rolling count over the last N seconds — smoother, with no boundary spikes. Token bucket: A bucket refills at a steady rate; each request spends a token. Allows short bursts, then throttles. The common choice. 429 + Retry-After: The polite ‘slow down' response, telling a client exactly how long to wait. Quotas (per day/month): Longer-window budgets for billing and fair use, layered on top of per-second limits. Load shedding: Under extreme load, drop low-priority requests entirely rather than rate-limit per client. Concurrency limits: Cap simultaneous in-flight requests instead of rate — good for protecting a slow backend.

chunks.title: Rate limiting — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Set the limit in each server's local memory and it silently multiplies: with 5 servers behind a load balancer, a ‘100/min' limit becomes 500/min, because each server counts only its own share. Set it too low and you throttle real users on a busy day. Forget the Retry-After header and clients hammer you the instant they're blocked, making the overload worse. Shared state and a sensible budget are everything. At small scale a simple in-process counter is fine. As you add server copies you must move the counter to a shared store (Redis). At very large scale, limiting moves to the edge — a CDN or API gateway rejects floods before they reach your servers — and budgets become distributed, each node enforcing a slice of the global limit.

chunks.title: Message queues
chunks.text: Handing slow or risky work to a line of messages, so the user never waits for it. A message queue lets one part of the system drop a job and reply instantly, while a separate worker does the slow work later — decoupling speed from reliability. A queue is a line of messages. Instead of doing a slow job inside the request (sending an email, notifying the kitchen), the backend writes a short message — ‘send receipt for order 42' — onto the queue and immediately tells the user ‘done'. A separate worker picks it up and does the real work. This decouples the fast path (answering the user) from the slow path (the actual work). The user's screen doesn't freeze waiting for an email server on the other side of the world. Queues also add durability: if the worker is down, messages wait safely in line instead of being lost, and get processed when it comes back. The alternative — doing everything synchronously inside the request — means the user waits for the slowest external thing, and a single downstream outage (the email provider) takes your checkout down with it. A queue absorbs spikes and survives outages. It also smooths load: a flood of orders becomes a long queue the workers drain steadily, instead of a thundering herd hitting a fragile downstream service all at once (backpressure). Producer: Whoever puts a message on the queue — here, the backend after taking an order. Broker: The queue itself (RabbitMQ, SQS, Kafka). It stores messages reliably until they're handled. Consumer / worker: A separate process that pulls messages, does the slow work, then acknowledges them. Ack & dead-letter: A message is removed only once the worker confirms success; repeat failures go to a dead-letter queue. Do it synchronously: Simplest, fine for fast critical work — but couples your speed and uptime to every dependency. Event streaming (Kafka): A durable log many consumers can replay — better for analytics and event-sourcing than a simple job queue. Cron / scheduled jobs: For work that's periodic rather than triggered by an event.

chunks.title: Message queues — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Forget that messages can be delivered twice and a retried ‘charge card' job double-charges the customer — queues demand idempotency. Let workers fall behind without monitoring and the queue grows for hours; users wonder why their receipt never arrived. Skip the dead-letter queue and one malformed message blocks everything behind it. A queue gives reliability only if the worker expects repeats and failures. At small scale you may not need a queue at all. As external work and traffic grow, a queue decouples and protects you. At large scale you run many workers in parallel (scaled independently of web servers), partition the queue by topic, and use streaming logs (Kafka) so fulfilment, analytics, and notifications each consume the same order events independently.

chunks.title: Sharding & replication
chunks.text: Splitting and copying a database so it can hold more data and survive failures. Replication makes copies of your data for safety and read speed; sharding splits it across machines so no single one has to hold it all. A single database server has limits — disk, memory, and queries per second. Two techniques push past them. Replication keeps full copies of the database in sync. Sharding splits the data into pieces, each on a different machine. Replication gives you read scaling and safety: many *replicas* answer read queries, and if the primary dies, a replica is promoted to take over. Writes still go to one primary. Sharding gives you write and storage scaling: the User table might split so users A–M live on shard 1 and N–Z on shard 2. No single machine holds everything, so you grow by adding shards. The alternative — one ever-bigger machine (vertical scaling) — eventually hits a hard ceiling and a single point of failure. Replication removes the single point of failure for reads; sharding removes the storage and write ceiling. Most systems reach for replication first (simpler, solves reads + availability) and only shard when one machine genuinely can't hold the data or absorb the writes — because sharding adds real complexity. Primary & replicas: One writable primary; read-only replicas kept in sync, ready to be promoted if it fails. Shard key: The column that decides which shard a row lives on (user id, region). Choosing it well is everything. Routing layer: Reads the shard key and sends each query to the right shard. Rebalancing: Moving data when you add shards — the hard, risky part of growing. Vertical scaling: Just buy a bigger box. Simplest, works surprisingly far, but has a ceiling and one failure domain. Caching + read replicas: Often removes the need to shard entirely by taking read load off the primary. NoSQL stores: Cassandra/DynamoDB shard automatically by design — at the cost of some relational guarantees.

chunks.title: Sharding & replication — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Choose a bad shard key and you get a hot shard: shard orders by date and today's shard takes all the writes while the rest sit idle. Cross-shard queries and transactions become slow and awkward — a join that was trivial now spans machines. Rebalancing a live, sharded database without downtime is one of the hardest jobs in infrastructure. Shard only when you must, and pick the key with great care. 10 users: one database, no replicas. Thousands: add read replicas and a cache to take read load off the primary. Millions with heavy writes: shard by a well-chosen key and accept cross-shard complexity. Planet-scale: globally distributed shards placed near users, with deliberate consistency trade-offs (CAP) on every cross-region operation.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Cloud compute — VMs, containers, serverless
chunks.title: Cloud compute — VMs, containers, serverless
chunks.text: The three ways to rent someone else's computers to run your code. From a whole rented machine (VM) to a sealed box (container) to just-a-function (serverless), cloud compute trades control for convenience — pick by how much you want to manage. ‘The cloud' is renting computers by the second instead of owning them. There are three main shapes, from most hands-on to least. A virtual machine (VM) is a whole simulated computer you rent and manage — you install everything on it. A container packs just your app and its dependencies into a sealed box that runs identically anywhere; many containers share one machine, so they're lighter and faster to start than VMs. (This is Docker; Kubernetes runs many of them.) Serverless (functions) goes furthest: you upload a function and the cloud runs it on demand, scaling to zero when idle and billing per call. There's still a server — you just never see or manage it. The choice is about how much undifferentiated heavy lifting you want to own. VMs maximise control and suit legacy or specialised workloads. Containers are the sweet spot for most services: portable, dense, orchestratable. Serverless is unbeatable for spiky or occasional work where paying for idle servers is wasteful. Owning physical servers (the old way) means buying for peak load and eating the cost when idle. Renting flips that — you pay for what you use and grow in seconds, not procurement cycles. VM: Full control of the OS; you patch, scale and secure it. Heaviest to run, slowest to start. Container: Just your app + deps, sealed and portable. Fast to start, dense, the modern default. Serverless: Just a function. Scales to zero, pay-per-call — but cold starts and time limits apply. Managed services: Rent the database/queue/cache itself, so you don't run it at all. On-prem / bare metal: Own the hardware. Cheapest at huge steady scale and maximal control, but you carry all the ops and capital cost. Platform-as-a-Service: Push code, the platform runs it (Heroku-style). Less control than containers, less work than VMs.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Cloud compute — VMs, containers, serverless
chunks.title: Cloud compute — VMs, containers, serverless — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Run everything on always-on VMs sized for peak traffic and you pay for idle capacity most of the day. Go all-in on serverless for a high-traffic, latency-sensitive service and cold starts and per-call costs bite. Treat containers as magic and forget that a crashing container restarts forever unless you watch it. Each model has a workload it's wrong for — match the shape to the traffic pattern. A side project runs cheaply on serverless or one small VM. A growing product standardises on containers + an orchestrator for portability and steady scaling. At massive scale you blend all three — containers for services, serverless for bursty glue, managed services for data — across multiple regions, optimising relentlessly for cost.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Web security — XSS, SQLi, SSRF
chunks.title: Web security — XSS, SQLi, SSRF
chunks.text: The classic ways web apps get broken — and the one habit that stops most of them. Most web attacks come from trusting input that should never be trusted; the fix is to treat all input as data, never as code. Almost every web vulnerability is a version of the same mistake: mixing untrusted input with trusted commands. Three classics show the pattern. XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) sneaks attacker JavaScript into a page so it runs in other users' browsers — stealing logins or defacing the page. SQL injection (SQLi) smuggles database commands into an input field. Build a query by gluing strings — "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'" — and an attacker types ' OR '1'='1 to read the whole table. SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) tricks your *server* into making requests it shouldn't — fetching an internal-only admin URL or cloud metadata endpoint — because it blindly trusted a user-supplied address. The thread through all three: the system confused *data the user gave* with *instructions to execute*. These defences are cheap and the attacks are devastating — a single SQLi can leak every customer record; one stored XSS can hijack every visitor. ‘Treat input as data' costs almost nothing and removes whole categories of bug at once. The alternative — trying to ‘clean' dangerous input by stripping bad characters (a blocklist) — is a losing game; attackers always find an encoding you forgot. Allow-listing and separating data from code are robust by design. Escape output (XSS): Render user text as text, never as HTML/JS. A strict Content-Security-Policy is the backstop. Parameterised queries (SQLi): Send the query and the values separately, so input can never become SQL. ORMs like Prisma do this for you. Allow-lists (SSRF): Only let the server fetch approved destinations; block internal IPs and metadata endpoints. Validate input: Reject anything that doesn't match the expected shape at the edge, before it reaches anything sensitive. Blocklist filtering: Trying to strip ‘bad' input. Brittle and bypassable — prefer parameterisation and escaping. A Web Application Firewall: A useful extra net that blocks known attack patterns, but never a substitute for fixing the code.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Web security — XSS, SQLi, SSRF
chunks.title: Web security — XSS, SQLi, SSRF — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Build one SQL query with string concatenation and your entire user table is one crafted input away from being dumped. Render one comment as raw HTML and an attacker's script runs in every reader's browser, stealing sessions. Let your server fetch any URL a user supplies and it may hand back your cloud's secret credentials. The damage is total and the fix is a habit: never let input become code. For a small app, parameterised queries, output escaping, and input validation cover the vast majority of risk. As you grow, add a Content-Security-Policy, security headers, dependency scanning, and least-privilege access so a breach in one place can't reach everything. At enterprise scale: threat modelling, regular pen-tests, secret rotation, and a WAF — but the foundation never changes: trust no input.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — What a program is
chunks.title: What a program is
chunks.text: Underneath every app you've ever used is the same thing: a list of instructions. A program is a precise list of instructions a computer follows, one at a time, exactly — no more, no less. Strip away the screens and the magic and a program is just a list of instructions, written down, that a computer carries out in order. The computer is breathtakingly fast and breathtakingly literal: it does *exactly* what the instructions say — even when that's not what you meant. Those instructions are written in a programming language — a set of words and rules precise enough that there's no ambiguity. English is too fuzzy (‘clean the room' means a hundred things); a program has to spell out every step. When you ‘run' a program, the computer starts at the first instruction and works down, sometimes looping back or branching depending on conditions. That's it. Everything else — apps, games, websites, AI — is built from this one idea, stacked very high. Why be this literal and precise? Because a computer has no judgement. Precision is the price of a machine that never tires, never improvises, and runs billions of these steps a second. The rigidity that makes programming hard is the same rigidity that makes computers reliable. Instructions: The individual steps — do this, then this. Run top to bottom. Conditions (if): ‘If this is true, do that' — how a program makes a decision. Loops: ‘Repeat this until done' — handling many things without writing each one out. Input & output: What it reads (a tap, a file) and what it produces (a screen, a saved order).

chunks.source: Tech Reference — What a program is
chunks.title: What a program is — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: The classic beginner's shock: the program does *exactly* what you wrote, not what you intended. Tell it to charge ‘the price' but forget to multiply by quantity, and every customer pays for a single burger no matter how many they ordered — forever, without complaint, until someone notices. The computer won't catch your mistake; it has no idea what you wanted.

chunks.title: Variables & memory
chunks.text: Where a program keeps the things it's thinking about right now. A variable is a labelled box in the computer's memory that holds one value your program can read and change. While a program runs it needs to remember things — a total, a name, whether the user is logged in. It keeps them in memory (RAM): a vast wall of tiny numbered slots the computer can read and write in an instant. A variable is a friendly name for one of those slots. Instead of ‘slot #4,891,233' you write cartTotal, and the language remembers which slot that is. You can read it (cartTotal) and change it (cartTotal = 250). Memory is fast but temporary — it's wiped when the program stops or the phone restarts. That's the crucial difference from a database, which remembers permanently. Variables are a scratchpad; the database is the filing cabinet. Without named variables you'd juggle raw memory addresses — unreadable and unmaintainable. Names turn memory into something humans can reason about. And keeping ‘right now' data in fast memory (not the database) is what makes apps feel instant; you only pay the slow cost of saving when something must persist. Value: What's currently in the box — a number, text, true/false, a list. Name: The label you gave it, so you and the code can find it again. Type: What kind of thing it holds — a number behaves differently from text. Scope: Where in the program the box exists. Most are cleared away when their little job finishes.

chunks.title: Variables & memory — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Confuse the scratchpad with the filing cabinet and you get the saddest bug: the user adds ten items, the app holds them in memory, the phone dies — and the cart is gone, because nothing was ever written to the database. Or two parts of the app keep their own cartTotal and drift apart. Knowing what lives in memory versus what's saved — and keeping one source of truth — is half of getting software right.

chunks.title: How code runs
chunks.text: The journey from the text you type to something a computer can actually do. Computers don't understand your code directly — it's first translated into the simple numeric instructions a processor executes. You write code in a human-friendly language, but a processor only understands machine code — bare numeric instructions like ‘add these two slots', ‘jump to here'. Something has to bridge that gap. There are two main ways. A compiler translates your whole program into machine code *ahead of time*, producing something the computer runs directly and fast. An interpreter reads and runs your code *line by line, as it goes* — slower, but flexible and quick to start. Many modern systems blend the two (‘just-in-time'): they start by interpreting, then compile the hot parts for speed. Dart does exactly this — interpreted while you develop (instant hot reload), compiled to native code when you ship. The trade is speed and safety vs flexibility and quickness-to-start. Compiling ahead of time gives you fast, checked programs — ideal for shipping. Interpreting gives instant feedback while developing. Knowing which is happening explains a lot: why some errors appear instantly and others only in production, and why ‘it builds' is a real milestone. Source code: The text you write, in a language made for humans. Compiler: Translates the whole program to machine code ahead of time. Fast to run. Interpreter: Runs your code line by line as it reads it. Flexible, quick to start. Machine code: The bare numeric instructions the processor actually executes.

chunks.title: How code runs — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Assume the computer grasps your intent and you'll be baffled when a tiny typo stops the whole program from building — the compiler can't run code it can't translate. Or, in an interpreted language, a mistake hides on a rarely-run line for months until the day it executes in front of a customer. Understanding the translation step tells you *when* your mistakes will be caught.

chunks.title: Offline-first & sync
chunks.text: Building an app that still works when the network doesn't. Offline-first treats the network as an unreliable luxury: the app reads and writes locally first, then syncs when it can. Phones lose signal — in lifts, on trains, in dead zones. An offline-first app is built so that losing the network is a non-event: it keeps working from a local copy of the data and quietly catches up with the server later. The core move is a local store on the device (a small database or cache). The app reads from it instantly and writes to it immediately, so the screen never waits on a flaky connection. A background sync reconciles local changes with the server when a connection returns. This flips the usual assumption. A naive app treats the server as the source of truth for every action; an offline-first app treats the *device* as good enough for now and the server as eventually-authoritative. The alternative — blocking every action on a live request — produces an app that spins, freezes, and loses work the instant the signal drops. For anything used on the move, offline-first is the difference between ‘usable' and ‘useless in a tunnel'. It also makes the happy path feel *faster*: reads and writes are local and instant, and the network cost is paid in the background, off the critical path. Local store: An on-device database/cache the app reads and writes instantly. Sync engine: Pushes local changes up and pulls server changes down when online. Conflict resolution: A rule for when the same thing changed in two places — last-write-wins, merge, or ask. Pending-write queue: Actions taken offline, held until they can be sent — and made idempotent so retries are safe.

chunks.title: Offline-first & sync — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Skip conflict handling and two devices editing the same record silently clobber each other — last writer wins, the other's work vanishes. Forget idempotency and a queued ‘place order' replays on reconnect, charging twice. Let the local store and server drift without a clear source-of-truth rule and the user sees different data on different devices. Offline-first is powerful but demands you take sync and conflicts seriously. A simple app might cache reads and queue a few writes. As it grows you need real conflict resolution, partial sync (don't pull everything), and schema versioning so old offline clients can't corrupt new data. At large scale this becomes its own discipline — CRDTs and sync engines that merge concurrent edits mathematically.

chunks.title: Object storage & CDNs
chunks.text: Where the world's files live — and how they reach users fast. Object storage holds files cheaply and durably by key; a CDN caches copies of them near users so they load fast everywhere. Databases are the wrong place for big files — images, video, backups, PDFs. Those go in object storage (like Amazon S3): cheap, effectively unlimited storage where each file is an ‘object' addressed by a key (a path-like name). Put a file in by key, get it back by key. Not a filesystem, not a database — a giant, durable key→file store. But a file in one data centre is slow for users on the other side of the planet. A CDN (Content Delivery Network) fixes that: it keeps cached copies of your files on servers all over the world, so each user is served from one nearby — cutting latency dramatically. Together they're how nearly every site delivers static assets: store once in object storage, serve everywhere via a CDN. Storing files in your database bloats it, slows backups, and costs far more than object storage. Serving them from a single region makes distant users wait. Object storage + CDN is cheaper, faster, and scales to huge traffic because the CDN absorbs the load your origin would otherwise take. It improves resilience too: the CDN keeps serving cached assets even if your origin has a hiccup. Object & key: A file plus its address (e.g. images/burger-42.jpg). Get and put by key. Buckets: Top-level containers that group objects and set access rules. Edge cache (CDN): Servers worldwide holding cached copies, serving the nearest user. Cache headers & TTL: Tell the CDN how long it may reuse a copy before re-checking the origin.

chunks.title: Object storage & CDNs — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Serve a file with a long cache time and then change it in place — users keep getting the old version for hours, because the CDN still has it (classic cache-invalidation pain). Make a private bucket public by accident and you've leaked data to the whole internet. Forget that the CDN caches by URL and you'll wonder why nobody sees your update. Versioned filenames and careful cache headers are the cure. A small site might serve a few images straight from object storage. As traffic grows, a CDN becomes essential to keep latency low and origin load down. At global scale you tune cache strategy per asset type, use signed URLs for private content, and lean on the CDN for the vast majority of traffic so the origin barely works.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — What a neural network computes
chunks.title: What a neural network computes
chunks.text: Underneath the AI hype is a stack of multiply-add-and-bend, repeated. A neural network is a big function that turns numbers into numbers by multiplying, adding and bending — and 'learning' is just nudging those numbers until its answers improve. Strip away the mystique and a neural network is a mathematical function: numbers go in (an image as pixels, text as numbers), numbers come out (a label, a probability, the next word). In between it repeatedly multiplies the inputs by weights, adds them up, and passes the result through a simple bending function (an activation) that lets it represent more than straight lines. Stack many such layers and the network can represent astonishingly complex relationships. The weights are the knobs — millions or billions of them — and they start random and meaningless. ‘Training' is the process of nudging those weights. Show the network an example, compare its answer to the right one, and adjust every weight a tiny bit in the direction that would have made the answer better (gradient descent, via backpropagation). Do that across millions of examples and the random knobs settle into something that works. Why this and not hand-written rules? Because for things like recognising a cat or continuing a sentence, nobody can write the rules — there are too many, too fuzzy. A neural network *learns* them from examples instead. The trade: it needs lots of data and compute, and its ‘reasoning' is opaque (millions of numbers, not readable logic). Modern language models are this idea at enormous scale, with a particular architecture — the transformer — that's especially good at sequences like text. Weights & biases: The millions of numbers that get tuned — the network's actual ‘knowledge'. Layers: Stages of multiply-add-bend; deeper stacks capture more complex patterns. Activation function: The ‘bend' that lets the network model non-linear relationships, not just straight lines. Loss & gradient descent: A score of how wrong it is, and the rule for nudging weights to lower it.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — What a neural network computes
chunks.title: What a neural network computes — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Train on biased or thin data and the network faithfully learns the bias — it has no judgement, only patterns. Ask it something outside what it saw and it may hallucinate a confident wrong answer, because it's pattern-matching, not looking anything up (which is exactly why grounding it with RAG matters). And because the ‘knowledge' is millions of opaque numbers, debugging a wrong answer is genuinely hard. Tiny networks run on a phone. Big ones need clusters of specialised chips (GPUs/TPUs) for days or weeks to train. Serving them at scale means optimising inference — batching requests, compressing the model, caching — because every answer costs real compute. The frontier is largely an engineering problem of training and serving these functions efficiently.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — API styles — REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets
chunks.title: API styles — REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets
chunks.text: Four ways for programs to talk — and when each one fits. REST, GraphQL, gRPC and WebSockets are different shapes of conversation between programs; the right one depends on who's talking and how. Once you have a backend, the question is *how* clients talk to it — and there's more than one answer. REST (which you've met) organises everything around resources at URLs, using plain HTTP verbs. Simple, universal, cacheable — the default for most web APIs. GraphQL flips control to the client: instead of many fixed endpoints, there's one endpoint and the client asks for exactly the fields it wants in a single query. Great when different screens need different slices of data and you want to avoid over- or under-fetching. gRPC is built for speed between *services* (backend-to-backend): compact binary messages and a strict contract, so internal calls are fast and typed. WebSockets open a permanent two-way channel, so the server can push updates the instant they happen — chat, live dashboards, multiplayer. Each exists because the others fall short somewhere. REST under-fetches (a screen needs three calls) or over-fetches (you get fields you ignore); GraphQL fixes that for rich, varied UIs. REST and GraphQL are too chatty for high-volume internal calls; gRPC is built for that. None of them push — so for anything live you reach for WebSockets (or server-sent events). Most real systems mix them: REST or GraphQL at the edge for clients, gRPC between internal services, WebSockets for the live bits. REST: Resources at URLs + HTTP verbs. Simple, cacheable, universal — the sensible default. GraphQL: One endpoint; the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one query. gRPC: Fast, typed binary calls between backend services. Not browser-native. WebSockets: A persistent two-way channel for real-time push (chat, live updates). Server-Sent Events (SSE): One-way server→client push over plain HTTP — simpler than WebSockets when you only need to receive. tRPC: Typed RPC for TypeScript-everywhere stacks — REST-like ergonomics with end-to-end types.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — API styles — REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets
chunks.title: API styles — REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Reach for GraphQL on a tiny app and you've added a query language, a schema, and caching headaches to a problem you didn't have. Expose gRPC straight to browsers and it won't work — it isn't browser-native. Hold thousands of idle WebSocket connections without planning for it and you exhaust server memory. And GraphQL's flexibility lets a client request a monstrously expensive query unless you add depth limits. Each style fits a situation, not a universal upgrade. A small product is well served by REST alone. As the front-end grows varied, GraphQL tames over-fetching. As you split into many backend services, gRPC keeps internal calls fast. At large scale you run all of them deliberately — an API gateway out front, a typed binary mesh inside, and a separate real-time tier for WebSockets — each scaled on its own.

chunks.title: CSS, layout & accessibility
chunks.text: Making a page look right for everyone — including people who can't see it. CSS controls how a page looks and lays out; accessibility makes sure that look works for every user, including those using a screen reader or keyboard. HTML says *what* is on a page (a heading, a button, a list); CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) says *how* it looks — colours, spacing, fonts, and how things arrange themselves as the screen changes size. It's a separate language from the HTML, so structure and styling stay independent. Modern layout is mostly two tools: Flexbox (arrange things in a row or column, distributing space) and Grid (two-dimensional layouts). With media queries, the same page rearranges itself for a phone, a tablet, or a wide monitor — that's responsive design. Accessibility (a11y) is the discipline of making sure all of that actually works for everyone — including people who navigate by keyboard, or who can't see the screen and rely on a screen reader that reads the page aloud. For many users it's the difference between using your app and being locked out. Separating CSS from HTML lets you restyle a whole site without touching its content, and reuse styles everywhere. Flexbox/Grid replaced a decade of hacks because they describe layout *intent* directly. And accessibility — beyond being right — is often a legal requirement, improves SEO, and (because semantic, keyboard-friendly pages are simply better-built) tends to improve the experience for everyone. The alternative — styling with inline hacks and div-soup, accessibility bolted on later — produces brittle layouts and apps that exclude real users. The cascade: Rules combine and override by specificity and order — the ‘C' in CSS. Powerful, occasionally maddening. Flexbox & Grid: The two layout engines: one-dimensional rows/columns, and two-dimensional grids. Media queries: ‘When the screen is this wide, change these styles' — the basis of responsive design. Semantic HTML & ARIA: Use the right element (button, nav, heading) so assistive tech understands the page; ARIA fills the gaps.

chunks.title: CSS, layout & accessibility — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Build buttons out of styled <div>s and a keyboard user can't reach them, a screen reader doesn't announce them, and your app is unusable for a chunk of people. Skip contrast checks and text vanishes for anyone in sunlight or with low vision. Forget alt text and images are silence to a screen reader. Lay out with fixed pixel widths and the page breaks on a phone. Most of this is invisible to a developer testing on their own laptop — which is exactly why it's so often shipped broken. A small site needs semantic HTML, responsive layout, and contrast — cheap and high-impact. As a product grows you add a design system of shared accessible components and automated a11y tests in CI. At large scale accessibility becomes a tracked requirement with audits and real screen-reader testing, because at a million users even a 1%-excluded edge case is ten thousand people shut out.

chunks.title: Managed databases & queues
chunks.text: Letting the cloud run your database, cache and queue so you don't have to. A managed service is infrastructure (a database, queue, cache) the cloud operates for you — you use it; they handle backups, patching, scaling and failover. Running a database yourself means installing it, configuring it, backing it up, patching security holes, monitoring it at 3am, and replacing the machine when it dies. A managed service hands all of that to the cloud provider: you get a database (or queue, or cache) as a ready-to-use endpoint, and they run the boring, critical operations behind it. Examples are everywhere: Amazon RDS or Cloud SQL (managed Postgres/MySQL), managed Redis, managed Kafka/SQS (queues). You connect and use them like the real thing — because they *are* the real thing, just operated for you. The trade is control for convenience and reliability. You give up some low-level tuning and pay a premium, and in return you stop spending your nights doing database operations. Operating stateful infrastructure correctly is genuinely hard and unforgiving — a botched backup or missed patch can lose or leak data. Most teams shouldn't reinvent that; a managed service buys battle-tested operations and frees your people for the product. Self-hosting makes sense at very large scale (cost) or for special needs, but for almost everyone the managed option is faster, safer, and cheaper once you count the human time. Managed database: Postgres/MySQL/Mongo run for you — automated backups, failover, version upgrades. Managed cache: A hosted Redis/Memcached, scaled and patched by the provider. Managed queue/stream: SQS, Kafka, Pub/Sub — durable messaging without running brokers yourself. What you still own: Your schema, queries and data model — they run the box, not your design.

chunks.title: Managed databases & queues — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Assume ‘managed' means ‘I don't have to think' and you'll still get burned: a bad query plan or a missing index is *your* problem, not the provider's. Outgrow your instance with no monitoring and you hit a wall mid-spike. Ignore the bill and convenience gets expensive. And you're now dependent on that provider — migrating a large managed database elsewhere is real work (lock-in). Managed removes the ops toil, not the need to understand your data. A small app leans entirely on managed services — one managed Postgres, a managed cache, done. As you grow you add read replicas and tune within the service. At very large scale, cost and control sometimes push the biggest players back to self-hosting parts of it with dedicated teams — but that's a deliberate trade made from a position of scale, not a default.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Cost, regions & availability zones
chunks.title: Cost, regions & availability zones
chunks.text: Where your servers live, and why the bill looks the way it does. Regions and zones decide how close and how resilient your system is; cloud pricing rewards understanding what you actually pay for. Cloud providers split the world into regions (geographic areas like ‘Europe-West') and each region into availability zones — separate data centres with independent power and network. Putting your system near your users cuts latency; spreading it across zones means one data-centre failure doesn't take you down. Where you run also shapes cost. You pay for compute by the second, storage by the gigabyte, and — the sneaky one — data transfer, especially data leaving a region (‘egress'). Two architectures that look identical can have very different bills depending on how data moves. Picking regions and zones, and understanding the pricing model, is part of designing a system — not an afterthought handed to finance. Latency and resilience are user-facing: a system in one distant zone is slow for far-away users and fragile if that zone hiccups. Multi-zone is the cheap insurance every serious system buys. Multi-region is the expensive insurance (and latency win) you buy when you truly need it. Cost-awareness matters because pay-per-use is double-edged: it scales down beautifully, but without attention it scales *up* your bill just as easily. Understanding what you pay for keeps the trade favourable. Region: A geographic area. Run near users for low latency; near data for compliance. Availability zone: An isolated data centre within a region. Span zones to survive one failing. Egress charges: Data leaving a region costs money — often the surprise on the bill. Pricing models: On-demand, reserved (commit for a discount), and spot (cheap but interruptible).

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Cost, regions & availability zones
chunks.title: Cost, regions & availability zones — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Run everything in a single zone and the day that data centre loses power, so does your product. Put your database in one region and your users on another continent, and every request crawls. Shuttle terabytes between regions without noticing and the egress bill dwarfs your compute. Forget to turn off a test cluster and it bills all month. The cloud doesn't protect you from your own architecture — geography and pricing are design decisions. A side project runs in one region, one zone, on-demand — fine. A real product spans multiple zones for resilience and right-sizes for cost. At global scale you run multiple regions with data-locality and compliance rules, blend reserved/spot capacity, and treat cost as a first-class engineering metric (FinOps) — because at scale a small per-request inefficiency becomes a very large number.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Training vs inference & cost
chunks.title: Training vs inference & cost
chunks.text: The two very different jobs in an AI system's life — and which one you pay for forever. Training is the expensive, one-off process of teaching a model; inference is running it to get answers — cheaper each time, but paid on every single request. An AI model has two phases. Training is teaching it: feeding huge datasets and adjusting billions of weights until it's good. It's enormously expensive — clusters of specialised chips running for days or weeks — but it happens relatively rarely. Inference is *using* the trained model: you give it an input, it does one forward pass, you get an answer. Each inference is far cheaper than training — but you do it on every request, forever. For a popular product, the lifetime cost of inference dwarfs the one-time cost of training. This split shapes everything about deploying AI. Training is a research-and-infrastructure problem; inference is a production-engineering and *cost* problem you live with every day. Most teams never train a large model from scratch — it's prohibitively expensive and rarely necessary. Instead they fine-tune or just call a pre-trained model via an API, turning a research problem into a manageable engineering one. Understanding the split keeps an AI feature viable: a clever product that costs more per answer than users will pay is a failed product. Inference cost is a core design constraint — part of why grounding with RAG (retrieve, then a cheap focused inference) often beats a giant model answering from memory. Training: One-off (or occasional) teaching of the model. Huge compute, lots of data, slow. Inference: Running the trained model per request. Cheaper each time — but constant. Fine-tuning: Cheaply adapting an existing trained model to your task, instead of training from scratch. Cost levers: Smaller/quantized models, batching, caching, and hosted API vs self-hosting.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Training vs inference & cost
chunks.title: Training vs inference & cost — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Confuse the two and you budget for AI like a one-time purchase, then watch inference costs balloon as usage grows — the bill scales with every request, not once. Pick a giant model when a small one would do and you pay for capability you don't use on every call. Skip caching and batching and you leave money on the table at scale. The model that's cheap to demo can be ruinous to run for a million users. Prototyping leans on a hosted API — no infrastructure, pay per token. As volume grows, inference cost dominates, so you optimise hard: smaller/quantized models, batching, caching, maybe self-hosting once the math favours it. Training from scratch only makes sense at the largest scale with a real reason; almost everyone fine-tunes or builds on someone else's trained model.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Secrets, rotation & least privilege
chunks.title: Secrets, rotation & least privilege
chunks.text: Keeping the keys to the kingdom out of your code — and limiting what each key can do. Secrets (passwords, API keys, tokens) must live outside your code, be rotated regularly, and grant the least access needed — so a leak is survivable. Every system has secrets: database passwords, API keys, signing keys, tokens. The cardinal rule is that they must never live in your code or get committed to your repo — because repos get shared, forked, and leaked, and a secret in git history is a secret out forever. Instead, secrets are supplied from outside — via environment variables or a dedicated secrets manager (like AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault) that stores them encrypted and hands them out only to the things that need them. Two practices make leaks survivable. Rotation: change secrets regularly (and immediately if one leaks), so an old stolen key stops working. Least privilege: give each key only the minimum access it needs, so a compromised key can't reach everything. Secrets are the highest-value target — one leaked database password can expose every customer. Keeping them out of code removes the most common leak path (the repo). Rotation limits how long a stolen secret is useful. Least privilege limits how much damage any single leak can do. Together they turn ‘catastrophe' into ‘contained incident'. The alternative — hard-coded, long-lived, broadly-scoped secrets — means one mistake (a public repo, a logged key) hands an attacker the whole system, indefinitely. Secrets manager: An encrypted vault that stores secrets and serves them to authorised services only. Environment variables: Secrets injected at runtime from outside the code — never hard-coded. Rotation: Regularly replacing secrets, and immediately revoking any that leak. Least privilege: Each key/role gets the minimum access it needs — shrinking the blast radius of a leak.

chunks.source: Tech Reference — Secrets, rotation & least privilege
chunks.title: Secrets, rotation & least privilege — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Commit an API key to a public repo and bots will find and abuse it within minutes — it happens constantly. Use one all-powerful database credential everywhere and a single leak exposes everything. Never rotate, and a key stolen years ago still works today. Log a secret to your monitoring system and you've leaked it to everyone with log access. The damage from secrets done wrong is total and fast; the discipline to do them right is cheap. A small app can use platform environment variables and rotate by hand. As you grow, a real secrets manager with access controls and automated, short-lived credentials becomes essential. At enterprise scale: per-service identities, automatic rotation, audit logs of every secret access, and least-privilege enforced everywhere — because the blast radius of one mistake grows with the system.

chunks.title: Threat modelling
chunks.text: Thinking like an attacker on purpose — before they do it for real. Threat modelling is the practice of systematically asking 'how could this be attacked?' so you find and fix weaknesses by design, not after a breach. Most security work is reactive — patch the hole after someone finds it. Threat modelling is proactive: you sit down, look at your system, and deliberately ask *how would someone attack this?* before shipping. It's a structured imagination exercise that turns ‘we hope it's secure' into ‘we've thought about how it breaks'. It revolves around a few questions: what are we building (a diagram), what can go wrong (the threats), what will we do about it (mitigations), and did we do a good job (review). The point is to find weaknesses on a whiteboard, where they're cheap to fix, instead of in production. A common lens is STRIDE — checking each part of the system for Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, and Elevation of privilege. It's a checklist so you don't forget a whole category of attack. Finding a design flaw on a whiteboard costs a meeting; finding it via a breach costs customers, data, and trust. Threat modelling shifts security *left* — earlier, where it's cheapest — and makes it systematic instead of relying on someone happening to think of an attack. The alternative — security as an afterthought, or a single penetration test right before launch — catches some things but misses design-level flaws that should never have been built. Data-flow diagram: A map of the system — components, data, and the trust boundaries between them. Trust boundaries: The lines where data crosses from less-trusted to more-trusted — the danger zones. STRIDE (or similar): A checklist of attack categories so no whole class of threat is forgotten. Mitigations & risk: For each plausible threat: how likely, how bad, and what we'll do about it.

chunks.title: Threat modelling — how it works & when it breaks
chunks.text: Skip it and you build whole categories of weakness in by design — an endpoint with no authorization check, a trust boundary you never noticed, a denial-of-service waiting to happen — and only discover them when an attacker does. Do it once and never revisit, and it goes stale as the system grows new attack surface. Treat it as box-ticking rather than genuine adversarial thinking and it finds nothing.
